guides.name: Everyday Protein
guides.descriptionText: Protein is one of the highest-impact food decisions. Compare common sources before you shop or plan meals.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Prefer plants and legumes when they work for the meal.
If you eat meat, smaller portions of chicken usually beat beef on footprint.
Look for certifications and pasture-raised claims when buying animal protein.
When you do buy meat, local pasture-raised from a farm you can ask about is easier to verify than a distant label. You get fresher product, less spoilage, and the money stays with nearby ranchers.
Local does not cancel beef's methane. A steak from down the road is still a high-impact meal compared with beans from anywhere.
Dried beans, lentils, and tofu from a regional mill or co-op keep plant protein cheap and easy.
guides.whatMattersMost: Land use, methane, and water dominate protein impact. Local helps transparency; it does not make beef low-impact.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating all meat as equal hides how much worse beef typically is than chicken or plants. Using “local” as a reason to eat more beef.

keyTypes.name: Beef
keyTypes.descriptionText: High greenhouse gas emissions from cattle farming and significant land use

keyTypes.name: Chicken
keyTypes.descriptionText: Moderate environmental impact, better than beef but still resource-intensive

keyTypes.name: Plant-based Protein
keyTypes.descriptionText: Lentils, beans, tofu - significantly lower environmental impact

guides.name: Seafood
guides.descriptionText: Use Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch when you shop: green is Best Choice, yellow is Good Alternative, and red is Avoid. Origin and fishing or farming method matter as much as the species.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Look up the species and country of origin on seafoodwatch.org before you buy.
Prefer Seafood Watch Best Choice (green) options such as U.S. farmed mussels, oysters, and clams, and Alaska wild salmon.
Yellow Good Alternative is fine when green is not available.
Skip red-rated seafood, including many imported farmed shrimp and bluefin tuna.
Ratings change — confirm the latest recommendation rather than memorizing a species.
Ask the counter what was landed nearby: freshness and a named boat are real benefits, and dockside sales keep money in the port.
Local is not automatically greener than a Seafood Watch Best Choice from farther away. A well-managed Alaska salmon often beats a depleted local stock.
Skip air-freighted “fresh” luxury fish. Frozen-at-sea green-rated fish usually has the better footprint.
guides.whatMattersMost: Stock health, bycatch, habitat, and farm pollution — Seafood Watch's three-color ratings summarize those. Nearby catch is a bonus when the rating is already green.
guides.commonPitfalls: The same fish can be green or red depending on where and how it was caught or farmed. “Salmon” or “shrimp” on a menu is not enough. Assuming the nearest harbor is the most sustainable.

keyTypes.name: Farmed Salmon
keyTypes.descriptionText: Seafood Watch often rates conventional open-net Atlantic salmon as Avoid or Good Alternative, depending on country and farm method. Pollution, escapes, and feed are the main issues.

keyTypes.name: Wild-caught Sustainable Fish
keyTypes.descriptionText: Choose wild fish that Seafood Watch rates Best Choice (green) or that carry MSC. Gear type and stock matter — pole-and-line tuna is a typical better pick than longline.

keyTypes.name: Alaska Wild Salmon
keyTypes.descriptionText: Seafood Watch generally rates Alaska wild salmon as Best Choice: well-managed stocks and lower habitat harm than many farmed salmon. Confirm the latest rating if labeled from another region.

keyTypes.name: U.S. Farmed Mussels & Oysters
keyTypes.descriptionText: Seafood Watch typically rates U.S. farmed bivalves Best Choice. They filter water, need no feed, and have a small footprint compared with fed fish.

keyTypes.name: Imported Farmed Shrimp
keyTypes.descriptionText: Many imported farmed shrimp sources are Seafood Watch Avoid (red) because of habitat loss, water pollution, and weak labor oversight. U.S. farmed shrimp is often a better alternative — check the origin.

keyTypes.name: Bluefin Tuna
keyTypes.descriptionText: Seafood Watch rates bluefin tuna Avoid. Stocks have been severely overfished. Choose other Seafood Watch green tuna options such as some pole-and-line skipjack instead.

guides.name: Milk
guides.descriptionText: Dairy versus plant milks is a frequent weekly purchase with a clear footprint gap.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Oat milk is typically the lower-impact everyday swap.
If you keep cow's milk, smaller amounts still help.
Check cartons for organic or regenerative claims, but volume used matters more.
A nearby dairy you trust on pasture and labor is a better carton than an anonymous national brand: shorter haul, fresher milk, and money stays with the farm.
Oat or soy drinks from a regional mill keep the plant-milk climate win and a shorter chain when you can find them.
guides.whatMattersMost: Cow's milk carries a much higher climate and land cost per liter. Local dairy improves freshness and farm pay; it does not match oat milk on climate.
guides.commonPitfalls: Buying extra local cream and cheese because it feels virtuous — dairy volume still dominates the carton.

keyTypes.name: Cow's Milk
keyTypes.descriptionText: Traditional dairy with high environmental footprint

keyTypes.name: Oat Milk
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plant-based alternative with significantly lower environmental impact

guides.name: Eggs
guides.descriptionText: Egg labels are mostly about animal welfare, with a smaller climate difference than meat swaps.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Choose pasture-raised or equivalent outdoor-access eggs when you buy eggs.
Avoid cheapest cage eggs if animal welfare is a priority.
Use what you buy; waste wipes out the benefit.
Farmers-market and farm-stand eggs are one of the easiest local wins: fresher eggs, you can see the flock, and the farmer is paid without a long wholesale chain.
Pasture and outdoor access still matter more than mileage alone — a nearby cage barn is not the point of buying local.
guides.whatMattersMost: Labor and animal welfare differ more than carbon between egg types. A local pasture flock is the clearest label you can get.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating “local” on a carton as proof of outdoor access. Letting eggs spoil after buying a flat at the market.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Eggs
keyTypes.descriptionText: Factory-farmed eggs with concerns about animal welfare

keyTypes.name: Pasture-Raised Eggs
keyTypes.descriptionText: Free-range eggs from chickens with outdoor access

guides.name: Coffee
guides.descriptionText: A daily habit: farming practices and farmer pay change the ethics of the same cup.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Look for Fair Trade, organic, or equivalent certifications.
Shade-grown and farmer-cooperative coffees usually score better on labor.
Brew at home in a reusable cup to cut waste.
Coffee beans do not grow in most of the U.S. “Local” here means a roaster who buys transparently from origin — not a claim that the coffee is regional.
A local roaster with Fair Trade, organic, or direct-trade lots beats supermarket mystery beans, and roasting nearby keeps the trail from farm to cup shorter after harvest.
guides.whatMattersMost: Labor standards and farming chemicals at origin, not just carbon per cup. Local roasting helps; it does not replace fair pay at the farm.
guides.commonPitfalls: Calling any neighborhood cafe “local coffee” while the beans are uncertified commodity lots.

keyTypes.name: Regular Coffee
keyTypes.descriptionText: Conventional coffee production with environmental concerns

keyTypes.name: Fair Trade Organic Coffee
keyTypes.descriptionText: Sustainably sourced with fair wages for farmers

guides.name: Produce
guides.descriptionText: Fruits and vegetables are where buying local and in season pays off most: flavor, farmer pay, less spoilage, and fewer miles on food that actually perishes.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Buy what is in season nearby first — farmers markets, CSAs, farm stands, and grocery produce labeled with a nearby farm or state.
Local seasonal food is picked riper, wastes less in trucks and warehouses, and puts money with the grower. You can ask how it was grown.
Transport is a small slice of most food's climate cost compared with beef or cheese, but it is a big deal for delicate, air-freighted produce: berries, asparagus, and stone fruit out of season.
Field-grown in a region that actually grows that crop, then trucked, usually beats a local heated greenhouse in winter for tomatoes and cucumbers.
Frozen vegetables packed at peak season are often as nutritious as “fresh” flown in, with far less spoilage.
Eating plants is the main win. Local and in season is how you get the best of that win.
guides.whatMattersMost: In season and nearby first. Air freight and heated glass in winter are the produce traps, not a truck from the next state.
guides.commonPitfalls: Assuming every local sticker is low-impact (winter hothouse tomatoes). Skipping frozen in-season vegetables for air-freighted “fresh.” Treating food miles as more important than eating plants instead of beef.

keyTypes.name: Local Seasonal Produce
keyTypes.descriptionText: Farmers markets, CSAs, farm stands, and nearby-field grocery produce in season. Picked riper, shorter haul, less spoilage, and you can ask how it was grown. Money stays with the farm. The climate win is modest next to skipping beef; the freshness, waste, and community wins are large.

keyTypes.name: Frozen In-Season Produce
keyTypes.descriptionText: Vegetables and fruit packed at peak season, often close to the field. Freezing uses energy, but you avoid air freight, winter hothouses, and the waste of “fresh” that spoils in transit. A strong off-season stand-in when the local stand is bare.

keyTypes.name: Regional Field-Grown Produce
keyTypes.descriptionText: In-season fruit and vegetables trucked from a growing region that actually produces them — most ordinary grocery produce. Field-grown plus a truck beat air freight and heated glass. Less transparent than a named local farm, still a solid everyday plant food.

keyTypes.name: Air-Freighted & Hothouse Produce
keyTypes.descriptionText: Berries, asparagus, and stone fruit flown in out of season, or tomatoes and cucumbers from heated greenhouses in winter. Transport or heating dominates. Flavor is usually worse than in-season local or frozen. Save these for a rare treat; they are not a weekly local-food substitute.

guides.name: Chocolate
guides.descriptionText: Cocoa is a labor and forest crop. Most of the world’s beans come from West Africa, where child labor and deforestation are well documented. A shorter, named supply chain beats a cheap bar with a rainforest on the wrapper.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Look for who grew it. Fair Trade, a cooperative name, or a bean-to-bar maker that publishes origin and farm pay beats a certification logo with no story. Direct trade is only meaningful if they actually publish prices, not a vibe.
Rainforest Alliance and similar mainstream marks are a floor, not a living income. Better than nothing on a grocery bar; not the same as a transparent small-batch maker.
Organic is about farming chemicals, not child labor. You can have both; you can also have organic cocoa from a weak labor chain.
Milk chocolate adds dairy. If you already cut cow’s milk for climate, dark with a short ingredient list is the smaller extra hit — see Milk.
Cheap candy is often little cocoa plus sugar, palm oil, and mystery “chocolatey” coating. Palm in fillings is a deforestation add-on. A smaller amount of real chocolate is the better habit.
Cadmium and lead can show up in cocoa solids. That is a reason to vary brands and skip eating baking chocolate by the pound, not to panic over a square. This is not medical advice.
Eat less, better. Cocoa’s ethical problems scale with volume. A good bar you taste is the point; a drawer of uncertified minis is not.
guides.whatMattersMost: Farmer pay and forests at origin — Fair Trade or a named transparent maker — then how much chocolate you actually eat.
guides.commonPitfalls: A rainforest cartoon on a commodity bar. Treating organic as fair labor. Volume of cheap Halloween candy as a rounding error. “Direct trade” with no published prices.
guides.searchTerms: chocolate,cocoa,cacao,fair trade,child labor,palm oil,bean to bar,candy,dark chocolate

keyTypes.name: Bean-to-Bar / Direct Trade
keyTypes.descriptionText: A maker who names origin, often a cooperative, and publishes what farmers were paid — or at least a short, traceable chain. Usually darker, less sugar, no palm filling. Costs more per ounce; you eat less. The labor and forest win is transparency plus volume, not a tasting-room vibe alone.

keyTypes.name: Fair Trade Chocolate
keyTypes.descriptionText: Fair Trade or equivalent (a real standard, not a house “ethically sourced” line). Premiums and rules on child labor and cooperatives. Not a perfect guarantee — audits miss things — but it is the strongest common grocery label. Pair with organic if you want both farming and pay covered.

keyTypes.name: Mass-Market Certified Cocoa
keyTypes.descriptionText: Rainforest Alliance or similar on a supermarket bar. Better than uncertified bulk cocoa; weaker than Fair Trade or a named direct-trade maker. Fine when it is what the store has. Do not treat the frog or tree logo as proof of a living wage.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Commodity Chocolate
keyTypes.descriptionText: Uncertified cocoa, mostly West African bulk, into everyday bars and chips. This is the system with the worst documented child labor and cocoa-driven deforestation. Taste can still be fine. The ethics problem is the default supply chain, not your dessert as a moral failing — buy less of this, or switch labels.

keyTypes.name: Cheap Candy “Chocolate”
keyTypes.descriptionText: Coatings, palm oil, sugar, and a little cocoa. Extra deforestation risk from palm, almost no farmer story, and a lot of volume at Halloween and checkout. Not a cocoa farmer’s product in any meaningful sense. A smaller Fair Trade bar beats a bag of uncertified minis.

guides.name: Cooking Oils
guides.descriptionText: The bottle on the stove is small next to palm oil hidden in snacks. Reuse fat you already have, then pick a temperate oil with a name. Unlabeled “vegetable oil” and cheap palm are the forest and labor problem.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Use what is already in the pan. Strain frying oil while it is still clean, keep it cool and dark, and stop when it smells off or smokes early. Leftover roasting fat from meat you already cooked is free oil — it is not a reason to cook extra meat (see Everyday Protein). Never pour grease down the drain; cool it and trash it, or take used oil to a biodiesel drop-off.
For a bottle: extra-virgin olive oil for cold use and moderate heat, or a named temperate seed oil (canola, sunflower, safflower) for high-heat frying. A short ingredient list — one oil — beats a blend. Origin on the label matters more than a leaf drawing.
Olive oil fraud is common: “Imported from Italy” can mean bottled there. Look for a harvest date, a country of crush, and a reasonable price. California and named Mediterranean estates are easier to trace than a mystery tin.
Canola and sunflower grown in temperate fields avoid tropical deforestation. They are farmed crops: fertilizer, pesticides, sometimes GMO. That is an agriculture choice, not a rainforest choice. Fine as the everyday fry oil.
Avocado oil is a luxury bottle. Avocado orchards can be water-hungry and, in some regions, tied to land clearing and violence. It is not a health or climate upgrade over olive. Buy it rarely, if the flavor is the point.
Palm oil yields a lot per acre, which is why it is in cookies, instant noodles, margarine, peanut butter, and cheap chocolate (see Chocolate). That yield is also why clearing peat and rainforest for it is so damaging, and why labor abuse shows up on plantations. RSPO or similar certified palm is a floor in packaged food you cannot avoid — not a green light to seek palm out. Conventional and unlabeled “vegetable oil” in junk food is the avoid list.
This is not medical advice. Smoke point and rancidity are cooking facts. Internet “seed oil” panic is not a forest ranking.
guides.whatMattersMost: Reuse first. Named olive or temperate seed oil for the bottle. Skip mystery vegetable oil and the snack aisle’s cheap palm.
guides.commonPitfalls: Dumping oil down the sink. Treating avocado oil as the ethical bottle. A rainforest logo on a cookie. Using “vegetable oil” without reading whether it is palm. Seed-oil discourse as a substitute for reading the label.
guides.searchTerms: cooking oil,olive oil,palm oil,canola,vegetable oil,avocado oil,sunflower,RSPO,frying oil,shortening,margarine

keyTypes.name: Reused Oil & Kitchen Fat
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact oil is already in the house. Filter still-clean frying oil, store it cool, and stop when it smells off. Drippings from meat you already cooked are leftover fat, not a climate-free pass to cook more meat. Cool grease and trash it or take it to a biodiesel drop-off — never the drain.

keyTypes.name: Extra Virgin Olive Oil
keyTypes.descriptionText: A temperate orchard crop: no tropical deforestation, a flavor you use as food not just grease. Water and migrant harvest labor vary by region. Fraud is the grocery risk — harvest date and a named origin beat a cheap “Italian” tin. Everyday bottle for dressings and moderate heat, not a reason to deep-fry gallons.

keyTypes.name: Temperate Seed Oil
keyTypes.descriptionText: Canola, sunflower, safflower — high-heat oils from fields that are not rainforest. Fertilizer, pesticides, and (often) GMO breeding are the real caveats, not orangutans. A named single oil beats a “vegetable oil” blend. The workhorse fry and roast bottle when olive is the wrong tool.

keyTypes.name: Avocado Oil
keyTypes.descriptionText: A trendy high-smoke bottle with a bigger water and land story than olive in many growing regions, plus documented clearing and violence in some avocado belts. Not a nutrition upgrade that erases that. Fine as an occasional flavor if you already like avocados — a poor everyday “better oil.”

keyTypes.name: Certified Palm in Packaged Food
keyTypes.descriptionText: RSPO or similar on a cookie, noodle, or spread you were going to buy anyway. Yield per acre is high, which is why palm is everywhere — and why leaked deforestation still happens on “certified” land. A floor, not a reason to seek palm out. Skip the snack if you can; read the label if you cannot.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Palm & Mystery Vegetable Oil
keyTypes.descriptionText: Uncertified palm, peat and rainforest clearing, and plantation labor abuse — often hiding as “vegetable oil” in cheap snacks, margarine, and candy (see Chocolate). High yield does not make this a climate win when the acre used to be a carbon store. The buying move is fewer of those products, not a different bottle of the same oil.

guides.name: Pasta
guides.descriptionText: A pantry staple where how the wheat was farmed matters more than where the box was packed.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Choose organic pasta when you can — it is the simplest way to avoid wheat sprayed with glyphosate just before harvest.
Italian organic brands (Bionaturae, Jovial) publish their sourcing; house brands rarely say anything about the wheat.
Whole wheat pasta adds fiber and nutrition; organic whole wheat avoids the residue trade-off that comes with conventional whole grain.
Treat instant noodle cups as a different food: the palm oil and the packaging, not the noodle, are the problem.
guides.whatMattersMost: Pre-harvest glyphosate desiccation and wheat farming practices. Pasta itself is a low-impact food; the farming is the footprint.
guides.commonPitfalls: Assuming “imported from Italy” says anything about how the wheat was grown — much Italian pasta is made from North American wheat.

keyTypes.name: Organic Pasta
keyTypes.descriptionText: Durum wheat pasta certified organic, typically Italian. No synthetic pesticides and no pre-harvest desiccation.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Dry Pasta
keyTypes.descriptionText: Standard supermarket pasta from conventionally farmed wheat. Cheap, shelf-stable, and a modest footprint — with the desiccant question unanswered.

keyTypes.name: Instant Noodles
keyTypes.descriptionText: Fried noodle blocks and cups, usually made with palm oil and sold in single-use packaging. The convenience is the cost.

guides.name: Bread
guides.descriptionText: A daily food where the healthiest-looking loaf can carry the most pesticide residue.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Certified organic bread is the cleanest signal — it addresses the wheat, not just the recipe.
A local bakery loaf skips the plastic bag and the preservatives, and you can ask where their flour comes from. Few will know — ask anyway.
Do not assume whole wheat beats white on every axis: conventional whole grain keeps the bran, and the bran is where glyphosate residue concentrates. Organic whole wheat gets both wins.
Short ingredient lists you recognize beat long ones with dough conditioners.
guides.whatMattersMost: The wheat itself — desiccation practices and residue — then packaging and food waste. Bread’s carbon footprint is small; its chemical footprint is the story.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating “whole wheat” as automatically the ethical pick, when conventional whole-grain loaves tested highest for glyphosate residue in Florida’s 2026 testing.

keyTypes.name: Organic Bread
keyTypes.descriptionText: Loaves from certified organic flour, whole grain or white. No desiccated wheat, no residue roulette.

keyTypes.name: Local Bakery Bread
keyTypes.descriptionText: Fresh loaves from a neighborhood bakery: no plastic, no preservatives, money stays local. Flour sourcing is usually the unknown.

keyTypes.name: Industrial Sliced Bread
keyTypes.descriptionText: Mass-produced sandwich loaves, white or conventional whole wheat. Consistent and cheap; the whole-wheat version carries the residue caveat in the guide.

guides.name: Breakfast Cereal
guides.descriptionText: A box that can be nearly plain grain or a dessert with a marketing department.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Plain oats — steel-cut or rolled, ideally organic — are the low-impact, low-sugar default.
Check sugar per serving before the front of the box: many “heart healthy” cereals are a quarter sugar.
Organic certification also answers the oat question: EWG testing repeatedly found glyphosate in conventional oat products.
Some big-brand cereals contain palm oil — one more reason the ingredient list beats the mascot.
guides.whatMattersMost: Sugar and processing first (health), then oat sourcing and palm oil. The box is a small footprint with a big health spread.
guides.commonPitfalls: Believing “made with whole grain” means mostly whole grain — it can sit behind sugar on the ingredient list.

keyTypes.name: Plain Oats & Oatmeal
keyTypes.descriptionText: Steel-cut or rolled oats, nothing added. A small footprint with no processing concerns; organic removes the glyphosate question.

keyTypes.name: Organic Boxed Cereal
keyTypes.descriptionText: Certified organic, low-sugar boxed cereals. Cleaner sourcing than conventional brands, still a processed, packaged food.

keyTypes.name: Sugary Big-Brand Cereal
keyTypes.descriptionText: High-sugar, heavily marketed cereals, some with palm oil. The health profile is dessert; the sourcing is opaque.

guides.name: Peanut Butter
guides.descriptionText: Peanuts are a humble legume — what brands add to them is where the ethics go wrong.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Two ingredients is the whole test: peanuts and salt. “Natural” on the label usually means it; check anyway.
If it contains palm oil, look for RSPO Identity Preserved or Segregated certification and a published mill list — or choose a brand that skips palm oil entirely.
Peanut butter does not need palm oil to work; the oil on top of a natural jar stirs back in.
Almond butter is not the upgrade it looks like — almonds are among the thirstiest crops grown in California.
guides.whatMattersMost: Palm oil sourcing. Peanuts themselves are low-carbon nitrogen fixers; the additive brings deforestation and, in the worst supply chains, forced labor.
guides.commonPitfalls: Paying more for “natural” conventional spreads that quietly still contain palm oil.

keyTypes.name: Natural Peanut Butter
keyTypes.descriptionText: Peanuts and salt, nothing else. No palm oil, no hydrogenation, no added sugar.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Peanut Butter (with Palm Oil)
keyTypes.descriptionText: The big shelf-stable brands: smooth, sweetened, and stabilized with palm oil of usually unstated origin.

keyTypes.name: Almond Butter
keyTypes.descriptionText: Often marketed as the premium healthy pick. Fine nutritionally; very thirsty to grow, and priced like it.

guides.name: Tea
guides.descriptionText: The world’s other daily cup, picked by some of the lowest-paid hands in agriculture.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Fairtrade or Fair for Life certification is the strongest signal on a tea box — plantation wages are tea’s core issue.
Loose leaf skips the bag, and many tea bags are plastic-lined and shed microplastics into the cup.
Worker-owned and cooperative estates exist and say so on the pack; commodity auction tea says nothing.
Bottled iced tea is mostly shipped water plus sugar in a plastic bottle — brew and chill your own.
guides.whatMattersMost: Plantation labor — wages and conditions in Assam, Kenya, and Sri Lanka — well ahead of the leaf’s small carbon footprint.
guides.commonPitfalls: Assuming a premium brand means premium labor standards; price and plantation pay are barely connected in tea.

keyTypes.name: Fair Trade Loose-Leaf Tea
keyTypes.descriptionText: Certified estates and cooperatives, sold loose. The labor standard is the point; the missing bag is a bonus.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Bagged Tea
keyTypes.descriptionText: Commodity auction tea in often plastic-lined bags. Convenient; the labor and the materials are both opaque.

keyTypes.name: Bottled Sweetened Iced Tea
keyTypes.descriptionText: Sugar water with tea flavor, in single-use plastic, trucked as a finished beverage. Every part of the footprint is the packaging and the sugar.

guides.name: Rice & Grains
guides.descriptionText: The base of most meals, where one grain’s growing method quietly outsizes the rest.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Rotate the base: oats, barley, millet, and buckwheat carry a fraction of rice’s footprint and most of its comfort.
When you buy rice, brown rice keeps more nutrition — and check origin; rice from drier regions and alternate-wetting methods carries less methane.
Rinse rice and vary grains for kids especially: rice concentrates arsenic from soil and water in a way other grains do not.
Quinoa’s price-spike story has largely settled; Andean-grown quinoa is a reasonable purchase, not a guilty one.
guides.whatMattersMost: Methane from flooded paddy fields — rice’s footprint per kilo runs several times that of other grains. Grain choice, not food miles, is the lever.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating all “ancient grains” as automatically low-impact regardless of how far they flew, or rice as just another grain.

keyTypes.name: Low-Impact Grains (Oats, Barley, Millet, Buckwheat)
keyTypes.descriptionText: Rain-fed temperate grains with small footprints and no paddy methane. The quiet overachievers of the pantry.

keyTypes.name: Brown Rice
keyTypes.descriptionText: Whole-grain rice: the same paddy methane, better nutrition, and slightly less processing loss than white.

keyTypes.name: Conventional White Rice
keyTypes.descriptionText: The global staple and the pantry’s methane heavyweight. Culturally central for billions — this guide suggests rotating it, not shaming it.

guides.name: Sodas
guides.descriptionText: Sweetened water with a supply chain: sugar, aluminum, and plastic, in that order.
guides.buyingAdvice:
The honest default swap is unsweetened sparkling water or seltzer — same ritual, no sugar, no sweetener debate.
If you buy soda, a can beats a plastic bottle (aluminum recycles well), and cane sugar beats high-fructose corn syrup mainly on farming, not on what it does to you.
Diet soda removes the sugar, not the acid on your teeth or the questions around sweeteners. It is a lesser harm, not a health drink.
Two-liter bottles and fountain cups are where the sugar quietly doubles. Portion is the footprint you control.
guides.whatMattersMost: Sugar — its health cost and the farming behind it — then the container. Soda’s carbon per can is modest; the lifetime habit is the impact.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating “craft” and “natural” sodas as healthy because the sugar is cane and the label is prettier. The sugar load is the same.

keyTypes.name: Sparkling Water & Seltzer
keyTypes.descriptionText: Unsweetened carbonated water, flavored or plain. The soda ritual without the sugar, sweeteners, or much of anything else.

keyTypes.name: Craft & Natural Soda
keyTypes.descriptionText: Small-batch sodas with cane sugar and prettier labels. The farming is a notch better; the sugar load on you is identical.

keyTypes.name: Diet Soda
keyTypes.descriptionText: Artificially sweetened soda. No sugar and no calories; the acid, the caffeine, and the open sweetener questions remain.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Cola & Soda
keyTypes.descriptionText: The big-brand default: HFCS or sugar, phosphoric acid, and a global sugar supply chain, in a can or a plastic bottle.

guides.name: Energy Drinks
guides.descriptionText: Caffeine wearing a racing suit — the drink is small, the marketing and the dose are not.
guides.buyingAdvice:
If the goal is alertness, coffee or tea delivers it with a known dose and a fraction of the packaging (see Coffee and Tea).
Check caffeine per can, not per serving — many cans are quietly two servings, and 200–300 mg cans are a drug dose, not a beverage.
Sugar-free versions remove the sugar crash, not the stimulant load or the marketing aimed at teenagers.
Energy shots concentrate the same caffeine into a plastic thimble — the worst ratio of dose to packaging in the aisle.
guides.whatMattersMost: Caffeine dose and who it is marketed to. The American Academy of Pediatrics says energy drinks have no place in children’s and adolescents’ diets at any dose.
guides.commonPitfalls: Reading “energy” as nutrition. The calories are sugar; the energy is caffeine, and caffeine borrowed is caffeine repaid.

keyTypes.name: “Natural” Energy Drink
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plant-caffeine energy drinks (green tea, yerba mate), often sugar-free. A gentler dose and label; still a stimulant product in a can.

keyTypes.name: Conventional Energy Drink
keyTypes.descriptionText: 160–300 mg of caffeine with sugar or sweeteners, sold with extreme-sports marketing that reaches plenty of teenagers.

keyTypes.name: Energy Shots
keyTypes.descriptionText: A full caffeine dose in two ounces of plastic. Maximum stimulant per sip, maximum packaging per milligram.

guides.name: Juice & Dried Fruit
guides.descriptionText: Fruit with the fiber removed or the water removed — convenient, and easier to overdo than the fruit it came from.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Whole fruit is the benchmark (see Produce). Juice keeps the sugar and drops the fiber — a glass of orange juice is four oranges you could not have eaten.
If you buy juice, 100% juice in the smallest carton you will finish; “juice drinks,” nectars, and cocktails are soda with a fruit picture.
Local fresh-pressed cider in season is the exception that earns its place: minimal processing, short trip, real orchards.
Dried fruit: unsweetened only. Check for added sugar and sulfur dioxide, and treat a handful as the serving — it is three plums, not a plum.
guides.whatMattersMost: What processing removed. Fiber and satiety go, sugar stays — juice’s health profile lands closer to soda than to fruit.
guides.commonPitfalls: Counting a juice drink as a serving of fruit, or dried fruit as a light snack by the open bag.

keyTypes.name: Local Fresh-Pressed Juice & Cider
keyTypes.descriptionText: Seasonal juice pressed near the orchard that grew it. Minimal processing, short trip, and a reason to exist beyond the carton.

keyTypes.name: 100% Fruit Juice
keyTypes.descriptionText: Real juice, nothing added — and still the fruit’s sugar without its fiber. A small glass is a serving; the carton is not.

keyTypes.name: Unsweetened Dried Fruit
keyTypes.descriptionText: Raisins, apricots, and figs with nothing added. Shelf-stable and waste-free; the sugar of three fruits in the space of one.

keyTypes.name: Sweetened Juice Drinks & Fruit Snacks
keyTypes.descriptionText: “Juice drinks,” nectars, fruit cups in syrup, and fruit snacks: typically 10–30% juice, the rest sugar water and marketing.

guides.name: Canned & Frozen Vegetables
guides.descriptionText: The processed side of the vegetable aisle — some of it is a costume, some of it quietly beats “fresh.”
guides.buyingAdvice:
Frozen vegetables packed at peak season are the budget superpower of this aisle: low waste, real nutrition, no air freight (see Produce).
Fermented and pickled vegetables — kimchi, sauerkraut, real pickles — add live cultures and keep for months in a jar, not a truck.
Canned is fine with two checks: BPA-free lining when it is stated, and a rinse to cut the sodium. Steel cans recycle well.
Vegetable chips and fries are potato chips in a costume: read them as snacks, not servings.
guides.whatMattersMost: How much of the vegetable survives processing, and what got added — sodium, sugar, and oil — on the way to the shelf.
guides.commonPitfalls: Paying fresh prices for veggie chips, or skipping frozen vegetables for tired “fresh” ones that traveled farther.

keyTypes.name: Frozen Vegetables
keyTypes.descriptionText: Vegetables frozen at peak season near where they grew. Less waste than fresh, no air freight, and nutrition that survives the freezer fine.

keyTypes.name: Fermented & Pickled Vegetables
keyTypes.descriptionText: Kimchi, sauerkraut, and real pickles. Preservation by microbes instead of trucks and freezers, with live cultures as a bonus.

keyTypes.name: Canned Vegetables
keyTypes.descriptionText: Shelf-stable and honest, with two caveats: can linings (look for BPA-free) and sodium (a rinse fixes much of it). Steel recycles well.

keyTypes.name: Veggie Chips & Fries
keyTypes.descriptionText: Packaged “vegetable” snacks that are mostly potato starch and oil — sometimes palm — wearing a vegetable costume.

guides.name: Light Bulbs
guides.descriptionText: Lighting is a simple swap: the same lamp, very different energy use and lifespan.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Choose LED for almost every household socket.
Match brightness in lumens, not watts.
Avoid the cheapest no-name LEDs if they fail early.
Recycle CFLs as hazardous waste because of mercury.
guides.whatMattersMost: Energy use and lifespan dominate lighting impact.
guides.commonPitfalls: Cheap LEDs with poor drivers fail early and erase the savings.

keyTypes.name: LED Bulb
keyTypes.descriptionText: Most energy-efficient lighting option with longest lifespan

keyTypes.name: CFL Bulb
keyTypes.descriptionText: Energy efficient but contains mercury and shorter lifespan than LED

keyTypes.name: Incandescent Bulb
keyTypes.descriptionText: Highly inefficient, converts most energy to heat rather than light

guides.name: Home Electricity
guides.descriptionText: Where your household power comes from is a high-leverage climate choice.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Rooftop solar pays off most with a long stay in the home.
If you cannot install panels, a renewable utility plan still helps.
Efficiency (LEDs, insulation) reduces how much power you need either way.
guides.whatMattersMost: Avoiding fossil-grid kilowatt-hours over the system's life.

keyTypes.name: Typical Grid Electricity
keyTypes.descriptionText: Household power from a mixed fossil and renewable grid

keyTypes.name: Home Solar Panels
keyTypes.descriptionText: Renewable energy source with high upfront cost but long-term savings

guides.name: Getting Around
guides.descriptionText: How you cover miles — commuting or traveling — is often a household's largest energy-related footprint.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Walk, bike, or e-bike when the trip allows it.
Prefer trains over planes where rail exists.
Local buses and trains beat driving alone for daily trips.
If you need a car, hybrid or electric beats a conventional gasoline vehicle.
guides.whatMattersMost: Miles traveled and fuel type, not brand.

keyTypes.name: Gasoline Car
keyTypes.descriptionText: Conventional engine with direct fossil fuel emissions for every mile

keyTypes.name: Plane
keyTypes.descriptionText: High climate cost per trip, especially short-haul flights that a train could replace

keyTypes.name: Hybrid Vehicle
keyTypes.descriptionText: Better than traditional gas but still uses fossil fuels

keyTypes.name: Electric Vehicle
keyTypes.descriptionText: Zero direct emissions, environmental impact depends on electricity source

keyTypes.name: Public Transportation
keyTypes.descriptionText: Local buses and mixed transit with lower per-person emissions than driving alone

keyTypes.name: Train
keyTypes.descriptionText: Intercity and commuter rail, especially electric, with very low emissions per passenger mile

keyTypes.name: E-Bike
keyTypes.descriptionText: Electric assist covers longer or hillier trips than a regular bike, with a small battery footprint

keyTypes.name: Bicycle
keyTypes.descriptionText: Zero emissions active transportation

guides.name: Smartphones
guides.descriptionText: Most of a phone's footprint is manufacturing, so keeping a device in use is the main win.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep your current phone if it still works.
Refurbished or certified pre-owned cuts mining and e-waste.
If you buy new, keep it for years and recycle the old one.
guides.whatMattersMost: Avoiding a new manufacture cycle.

keyTypes.name: New Smartphone
keyTypes.descriptionText: High environmental cost from rare mineral extraction and manufacturing

keyTypes.name: Refurbished Smartphone
keyTypes.descriptionText: Extends device lifecycle, significantly reduces e-waste and new production

guides.name: Water Bottles
guides.descriptionText: A reusable bottle replaces a long chain of single-use plastic.
guides.buyingAdvice:
One durable bottle you actually carry beats a cupboard of extras.
Skip single-use plastic for everyday water.
Stainless or quality plastic both work if you use them for years.
guides.whatMattersMost: Avoiding repeated single-use bottles.

keyTypes.name: Single-use Plastic Bottles
keyTypes.descriptionText: Major contributor to ocean plastic pollution and microplastics

keyTypes.name: Reusable Water Bottle
keyTypes.descriptionText: Eliminates single-use plastic waste, pays for itself over time

guides.name: Household Cleaners
guides.descriptionText: Cleaners affect indoor air, waterways, and packaging waste.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Pick plant-based, biodegradable formulas when they still clean well.
Concentrates and refills cut packaging.
You rarely need a different bottle for every room.
guides.whatMattersMost: Ingredients that reach water, plus packaging.

keyTypes.name: Conventional All-Purpose Cleaner
keyTypes.descriptionText: Chemical-based cleaner with environmental concerns

keyTypes.name: Eco-Friendly All-Purpose Cleaner
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plant-based, biodegradable cleaning solution

guides.name: Shopping Bags
guides.descriptionText: Bags are a habit purchase: reuse is the whole game.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep a reusable bag where you will actually remember it.
A bag used hundreds of times beats plastic, paper, and an unused cotton tote.
Paper is a better one-off than plastic if you forgot a reusable, but it still costs water and energy to make.
Avoid taking new bags 'just in case' every trip.
guides.whatMattersMost: Reuse count, not the material of an unused bag.

keyTypes.name: Plastic Shopping Bag
keyTypes.descriptionText: Single-use plastic contributing to ocean pollution

keyTypes.name: Paper Shopping Bag
keyTypes.descriptionText: Avoids plastic pollution but is water- and energy-intensive to make, and still usually single-use

keyTypes.name: Reusable Shopping Bag
keyTypes.descriptionText: Durable bag replacing hundreds of single-use bags

guides.name: Clothing
guides.descriptionText: A buying guide for garments: how they are made, how long they last, and who sews them. For fibers that work in heat, cold, or on the trail, open Summer, Winter, or Outdoor Clothing.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Wear what you already own first, and buy less often.
Secondhand usually wins on footprint; inspect quality so it actually lasts.
For new clothes, look for GOTS, Fair Trade, or living-wage brands and fibers you will wear for years.
Match the fiber to the season: linen and lyocell for heat, wool and down for cold, merino and a real rain shell outdoors — see those guides for the material comparison.
Avoid trend pieces you will discard after a season.
Repair and tailor instead of replacing when you can.
guides.whatMattersMost: How often you wear it, plus labor and fiber — not the brand logo.
guides.commonPitfalls: Organic cotton is better farming, but a closet full of new organic tees still costs water and carbon.

keyTypes.name: Fast Fashion
keyTypes.descriptionText: Low-cost clothing with poor labor practices and high environmental impact

keyTypes.name: Organic Cotton
keyTypes.descriptionText: Grown without harmful pesticides, better for soil and workers, but still water-intensive if you buy a lot of new garments

keyTypes.name: Sustainable Fashion
keyTypes.descriptionText: Eco-friendly materials, fair labor practices, and durability focus

keyTypes.name: Secondhand/Thrifted
keyTypes.descriptionText: Extends clothing lifecycle, minimal new resource consumption. Quality varies, so inspect wear.

guides.name: Summer Clothing
guides.descriptionText: Stay cool, dry, and sun-safe. Plant fibers that breathe usually beat synthetics for everyday heat; save polyester for sport.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Loose weave and a loose cut beat a tight shirt in heat, whatever the fiber.
Linen and hemp breathe, dry quickly, and need far less irrigation than cotton. Wrinkles are the tradeoff, not a defect.
Lyocell (often sold as Tencel) feels cool and drapes well. That win is the closed-loop process — generic viscose or rayon is not the same fiber.
Lightweight merino for travel and humidity: it handles sweat, resists odor, and you pack fewer shirts.
Light cotton is fine for dry, casual heat if you will wear it for years. Once you sweat, cotton stays wet, heavy, and slow to dry. Prefer organic if you buy new.
Save polyester for running or cycling. It wicks and dries fast, sheds microplastics, and smells sooner. Prefer recycled content and wash in a fiber-catching bag.
Light colors and a tight enough weave for UPF beat a dark, clingy tee plus extra sunscreen. For lotions, open the Sunscreens guide.
Buy used first. One linen shirt you wear every summer beats three new “breathable” fashion pieces.
guides.whatMattersMost: Breathability and dry time in heat; then water, pesticides, and how many summers you will actually wear it.
guides.commonPitfalls: Heavy denim, lined synthetics, and black polyester tees in humid heat. Calling any viscose “Tencel.” Buying a new summer wardrobe instead of a few fibers that work.

keyTypes.name: Linen
keyTypes.descriptionText: Flax needs little irrigation compared with cotton. A loose linen weave is one of the coolest summer fabrics: it breathes, dries fast, and does not cling when you sweat. Wrinkles easily. Best for shirts, trousers, and dresses in heat — not for hard rain or high-output sport.

keyTypes.name: Hemp
keyTypes.descriptionText: Similar summer performance to linen: breathable, durable, and low-pesticide if grown well. Starts stiffer than linen and softens with wear. Good for hot-weather shirts and pants you will keep for years. Blends with cotton or lyocell if you want a gentler hand.

keyTypes.name: Lyocell (Tencel)
keyTypes.descriptionText: Wood-pulp fiber made in a closed loop, so solvent is reused. Cool against skin, moisture-managing, and less thirsty than cotton — a strong everyday summer choice for shirts and dresses. Confirm it is lyocell/Tencel, not conventional viscose or rayon, which uses a dirtier chemical process.

keyTypes.name: Lightweight Merino
keyTypes.descriptionText: Fine wool that regulates temperature in heat as well as cool mornings. Moves sweat, resists odor, and lets you pack fewer summer shirts — the travel case. Sheep methane and grazing are the impact cost; offset that by wearing it for years and looking for Responsible Wool Standard. Not a linen substitute for sitting still in blazing sun.

keyTypes.name: Lightweight Cotton
keyTypes.descriptionText: Breathable in dry heat while you are at rest, familiar, and easy to find used. Holds water once you sweat, so it stays heavy and slow to dry in humidity. Farming is water- and pesticide-intensive unless organic. Fine for casual summer if the garment is light, you will wear it for years, and you skip a closet of new tees.

keyTypes.name: Recycled Athletic Polyester
keyTypes.descriptionText: The summer sport fiber: wicks, dries fast, and survives wash-and-sweat cycles. Poor everyday lounge wear in heat — it can feel clammy at rest, holds odor, and sheds microplastics. Recycled content is better than virgin. Use it for running and cycling, not as your only hot-weather wardrobe.

guides.name: Winter Clothing
guides.descriptionText: Warmth is layers plus a fiber that still insulates when you are damp. Cotton next to the skin in the cold is a comfort and safety miss.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Dress in layers: a thin base, an insulating midlayer, and a wind or rain shell you can vent. One huge fashion coat is harder to tune.
Wool — especially merino next to skin — stays warm when damp and resists odor. Look for Responsible Wool Standard or equivalent, and buy used when the knit is sound.
Down is the lightest warmth if you can keep it dry. Choose RDS or Responsible Down, and treat it as indoor-to-dry-cold kit, not a rain coat.
Wet winters, sweaty commutes, and soggy snow: recycled synthetic insulation (PrimaLoft-type) keeps loft when damp. Virgin polyester fill is the same warmth with a worse footprint.
Fleece is a workhorse midlayer. Recycled polyester is the better buy; it still sheds microfibers, so wash less often and use a catch bag.
Skip cotton as a base layer or the only sweater in wet cold. It holds water and pulls heat. A cotton hoodie is indoor clothing.
Repair zippers, re-proof shells, and re-stitch seams. A decade in one parka beats a cheap new coat every December.
Secondhand wool and down are the lowest-impact warm clothes you can buy.
guides.whatMattersMost: Insulation when damp, then years of use. Fiber and construction beat a brand’s winter campaign.
guides.commonPitfalls: Cotton thermals, fashion puffers that wet out, and three mediocre coats instead of one repairable system. Down in a rainy commute with no shell.

keyTypes.name: Wool Sweaters & Base Layers
keyTypes.descriptionText: The winter workhorse. Wool insulates when damp, which cotton does not. Merino next to skin for a base layer; a denser knit as a sweater or midlayer. Renewable if sheep are managed well — look for RWS and buy used when the garment is sound. Can itch in coarse grades; merino usually does not.

keyTypes.name: Responsible Down
keyTypes.descriptionText: Highest warmth for the least weight and pack size — the best dry-cold puffy. Collapses when soaked, so pair it with a shell in wet weather. Animal welfare depends on the supply chain: RDS or Responsible Down Standard, not unlabeled bargain fill. A repaired down parka worn for a decade beats a new synthetic coat every winter.

keyTypes.name: Recycled Synthetic Insulation
keyTypes.descriptionText: PrimaLoft-type polyester fill that keeps loft when wet — the right puffy for rainy winters, sweaty commutes, and soggy snow. Heavier and bulkier than down for the same warmth. Recycled content cuts the virgin-plastic hit; it still sheds fibers. Skip unlabeled cheap fill that mats after a season.

keyTypes.name: Recycled Fleece Midlayer
keyTypes.descriptionText: Warm, fast-drying, and easy to vent — a standard winter midlayer under a shell. Wind cuts through it, so it is not a jacket on a cold, exposed day. Recycled polyester is the better buy. Washes release microfibers; wash cold, less often, and use a catch bag. Secondhand fleece is widely available.

keyTypes.name: Cotton in the Cold
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cotton hoodies, flannel, and denim are indoor or dry-city clothes. As a winter base layer or the only sweater in wet cold, cotton holds water and pulls heat — the opposite of what insulation should do. High water to grow, and it fails the job you bought it for. Keep it for the house; wear wool or synthetics outside.

guides.name: Outdoor Clothing
guides.descriptionText: Hiking, camping, and wet wind need a layering system: base, insulation, weather shell. Cotton for activity is a safety problem, not just an ethics one.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Build layers you can add or dump: base against skin, insulation, then a shell for rain or hard wind.
Base layer: merino for odor and a wide temperature range; polyester or nylon if you want the fastest dry and will wash more often.
Never cotton on the move. Wet cotton stays cold, heavy, and slow to dry — a real risk in wind or shoulder season.
Rain: one waterproof-breathable shell with taped seams. Prefer a recycled face fabric and PFAS-free DWR. Fashion raincoats without seam tape leak at the first stitch line. A vinyl poncho is emergency kit, not hiking kit.
Wind without rain: a light windshirt or softshell vents better than hiding in a rain shell all day.
Insulation on the trail is the same as winter — fleece or a light puffy over the base. Down if the forecast is dry; synthetic fill if you expect sweat and showers.
Repair tape, replacement zippers, and re-waterproofing are how outdoor gear earns its footprint. Manufacturing dominates; years of use are the win.
Skip extra branded “trail” outfits. Two merino tops, one midlayer, and one real shell cover most trips.
guides.whatMattersMost: A layering system that keeps you dry and warm in motion — merino or synthetic next to skin, never cotton, plus one competent shell.
guides.commonPitfalls: Cotton hiking tees, untaped fashion rain jackets, and three cheap shells instead of one you repair. Wearing a rain jacket as a sweatshirt in dry cold.

keyTypes.name: Merino Base Layer
keyTypes.descriptionText: The outdoor next-to-skin layer that works across the most days: moves sweat, resists odor on multi-day trips, and stays useful from cool mornings to hard climbs. Prefer midweight for cold starts, lightweight for summer hiking. Look for RWS. Costs more up front; fewer shirts and fewer washes are the payoff.

keyTypes.name: Synthetic Base Layer
keyTypes.descriptionText: Polyester or nylon against the skin dries faster than merino and costs less — useful in very wet activity if you will wash it often. Holds odor, sheds microplastics, and feels worse at rest. Recycled content is the better version. A solid alternative when merino is out of budget or you run hot and soak shirts.

keyTypes.name: Waterproof Breathable Shell
keyTypes.descriptionText: The rain and wet-wind layer: taped seams, a membrane (ePTFE, PU, or similar), and a DWR face. One durable shell you re-proof is the outdoor buy — not three fashion raincoats. Prefer recycled face fabric and PFAS-free DWR. Untaped seams leak. Manufacturing is the footprint; years of repairs are how you justify it.

keyTypes.name: Softshell & Windshirt
keyTypes.descriptionText: For wind and light spray when it is not truly raining. More breathable than a rain shell, so you overheat less on the move. A light windshirt packs small; a stretch softshell adds light insulation. Not a substitute for taped waterproofs in hours of rain. Recycled nylon or polyester faces are widely available.

keyTypes.name: Cotton for Hiking
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cotton tees and sweatshirts on the trail hold rain and sweat, dry slowly, and chill you in wind — the old “cotton kills” warning. High water to grow, and they fail as outdoor clothing. Save cotton for camp in dry weather or the ride home. On the move, wear merino or synthetic.

guides.name: Shoes
guides.descriptionText: Footwear has its own materials and animal-product questions, separate from apparel.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Repair and resole before replacing.
If you buy new, longer-lasting pairs beat cheap pairs that fail in a season.
Plant-based and recycled designs avoid cattle-linked leather impacts.
guides.whatMattersMost: Materials and how many pairs you actually wear out.

keyTypes.name: Leather Shoes
keyTypes.descriptionText: Traditional leather with high environmental cost from cattle industry

keyTypes.name: Vegan Sustainable Shoes
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plant-based materials with circular design

guides.name: Kayaks
guides.descriptionText: Pick the hull for the water you actually paddle, then the material. Length, rocker, and weight decide tracking, turning, and how hard the boat is to paddle — construction decides durability and footprint.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Match the boat to conditions first: flat water, whitewater, or rough water (ocean and large windy lakes).
Length: shorter kayaks (about 6–12 ft) turn easily and feel playful but are slower and get pushed around by wind. Longer kayaks (about 14–18 ft) track straighter, hold speed, and handle chop better, but they are harder to spin.
Rocker (the curve of the keel): high rocker rides over waves and pivots in current — what whitewater boats need. Low rocker tracks into the wind and covers distance — what touring and sea kayaks need.
Maneuverability vs tracking: you rarely get both. A short, high-rocker hull is maneuverable; a long, low-rocker hull with a skeg or rudder tracks.
Ease of paddling: lighter boats and longer waterlines take less effort once moving. Heavy rotomolded polyethylene is stable and tough but more work to paddle, carry, and car-top.
Whitewater: short, high-rocker, rotomolded polyethylene. Other materials crack or delaminate on rocks.
Flat water: recreational lengths, moderate rocker, polyethylene, thermoformed ABS, or inflatables if storage is the constraint.
Touring kayaks: usually long (about 14–18 ft), low rocker, and fitted with multiple large watertight bulkheads. Bulkheads keep the boat afloat if you capsize and give dry storage for camping gear. Look for at least a front and rear bulkhead, plus a skeg or rudder for wind. A rec boat without bulkheads is not a touring boat.
Rough water: long touring or sea kayaks, low rocker, composites, wood, or long polyethylene; add a skeg or rudder for wind.
Buy used if the hull is sound.
Prefer recycled-content polyethylene for a new plastic boat you will keep for years.
Skip cheap PVC inflatables unless you paddle rarely and need closet storage.
Fiberglass and carbon only pay off if you paddle often for a decade or more.
Wood is renewable if you maintain varnish and repairs.
guides.whatMattersMost: Water type, length, and rocker first; then material. Touring needs length, low rocker, and real bulkheads — not just a long recreational hull.
guides.commonPitfalls: Buying a long sea kayak for a small pond, or a whitewater playboat for a windy crossing. Calling a 12 ft rec boat a touring kayak because it has a hatch — touring needs length, low rocker, and multiple large bulkheads. An unused carbon race boat still carries a large manufacturing footprint.

keyTypes.name: Inflatable PVC Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Best on calm flat water. Soft hulls are slower, wander in wind, and do not track well. Easy to paddle only because they are light to carry, not because they are efficient. Poor choice for whitewater or rough lakes. PVC chemistry and short life remain the impact problem.

keyTypes.name: Rotomolded Polyethylene Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: The standard whitewater material: short, high-rocker playboats and creek boats survive rocks. Recreational rotomold (about 9–12 ft, moderate rocker) suits flat water but is heavy, so it is harder to paddle and car-top. Longer PE touring hulls can handle chop if they are long, low-rocker, and have multiple large bulkheads; they still track less well than composites. Tough, fossil-based, and built to last.

keyTypes.name: Thermoformed Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Usually recreational and light-touring lengths for flat water and mild chop — not whitewater. Lighter and stiffer than rotomold, so easier to paddle and quicker to speed. Moderate rocker; longer thermoform hulls track decently, shorter ones turn more easily. Scratches, UV, and hard impacts are the durability limits.

keyTypes.name: Recycled Polyethylene Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Same handling as other rotomolded polyethylene: whitewater if short and rockered, flat-water rec if mid-length, touring if long, low-rocker, and bulkheaded. Still heavy to paddle compared with composites. Recycled content is the impact win, not a change in how the boat moves.

keyTypes.name: Fiberglass Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Common for touring and sea kayaks: long (often 14–18 ft), low rocker, efficient waterline, and multiple large bulkheads for flotation and dry gear. Easier to paddle than heavy polyethylene because the boat is lighter and holds speed in wind and chop. Turns slowly — that tracking is the point. Not for whitewater; rocks crack gelcoat and fiberglass.

keyTypes.name: Carbon Fiber Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Lightest paddle stroke and best for long, low-rocker sea and racing hulls in rough water or into the wind. Serious touring boats add multiple large bulkheads plus a skeg or rudder. Highly efficient once moving; not maneuverable in the whitewater sense. Fragile on rocks. High manufacturing energy — only sensible if you paddle hard for many years.

keyTypes.name: Wooden Kayak
keyTypes.descriptionText: Often built as touring or sea kayaks: longer hulls (about 14–18 ft), modest rocker, good tracking in wind and open water, and bulkheads for safety and camping gear. Easier to paddle than rotomold if kept light, and very maneuverable only if built short. Needs varnish care. Not a whitewater boat unless specifically designed and reinforced.

guides.name: Sunscreens
guides.descriptionText: Sun protection is clothing and shade first, then a lotion you will actually reapply. Read the active ingredients — mineral zinc is the usual better pick for skin, kids, and reefs; oxybenzone formulas and aerosol sprays are the ones to skip.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Cover up first: UPF shirt, hat, and shade. Sunscreen is for the skin that still sees sun.
Broad spectrum (UVA and UVB). SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB; SPF 50 about 98%. SPF 100 is not twice as protective and often means you put on too little.
Use enough — about a shot-glass for a body, a nickel for a face — and reapply every two hours, and after swimming or heavy sweat. Water resistant 40 or 80 minutes is not waterproof.
Mineral lotions with non-nano zinc oxide sit on the skin instead of soaking in. Best for face, kids, sensitive skin, and near coral. A tinted zinc cuts the white cast.
Titanium dioxide is also mineral. Fine in a lotion; skip inhaling spray or powder forms.
If you use a chemical filter, pick one without oxybenzone or octinoxate. Those two are banned on some reefs (Hawaii, Palau, U.S. Virgin Islands) and are the main hormone and allergy concerns.
“Reef safe” on the bottle is unregulated marketing. Read the Drug Facts actives.
Skip aerosol sprays: you rarely get even coverage, you inhale propellant, and most of it never lands on skin. A stick is better for ears, nose, and kids’ faces.
Do not buy a sunscreen–bug-repellent combo — you reapply them on different schedules. See Bug Repellents for DEET, picaridin, and permethrin.
Check the expiry. An old bottle in a hot car is not doing the job.
guides.whatMattersMost: Enough product, reapplied, with zinc oxide or a chemical formula that skips oxybenzone and octinoxate. Clothing still beats any bottle.
guides.commonPitfalls: SPF 100 as a substitute for reapplying. “Reef safe” with oxybenzone in the Drug Facts. Spraying a cloud and calling it covered. Combining sunscreen with insect repellent.

keyTypes.name: Non-nano Zinc Oxide
keyTypes.descriptionText: The best everyday active: zinc oxide is mineral, broad spectrum, and stays on the skin instead of absorbing. Non-nano is the reef-kinder particle size. Use a lotion or stick, not a spray. Tinted formulas cut the white cast on face and neck. Reapply like any sunscreen — zinc is not all-day armor.

keyTypes.name: Titanium Dioxide Mineral
keyTypes.descriptionText: Also mineral, often blended with zinc. Strong on UVB, a bit weaker alone on UVA, so look for zinc in the same Drug Facts. Fine in a cream. Skip sprays and powders — inhaling titanium dioxide is the concern, not wearing it on skin. Can leave a white or ashy cast.

keyTypes.name: Oxybenzone-Free Chemical
keyTypes.descriptionText: Filters such as avobenzone, octisalate, homosalate, or octocrylene absorb UV rather than sitting on top. Often thinner and clearer than zinc, so people actually use enough. Skip oxybenzone and octinoxate. Still washes into water; not the reef pick. Reapply on the same schedule as mineral.

keyTypes.name: Oxybenzone & Octinoxate
keyTypes.descriptionText: Older chemical filters still common in cheap lotions and sprays. Banned for reef sale in Hawaii, Palau, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Higher allergy and hormone-disruption concern than zinc or newer filters. If either name is in the Drug Facts, pick another bottle — “reef safe” on the front does not override the label.

keyTypes.name: Aerosol Spray Sunscreen
keyTypes.descriptionText: Easy to under-apply: much of the cloud misses skin, and you inhale propellant and leftover filter. Fire hazard near grills. Extra packaging and wasted product. If a spray is all you have, spray into your hands and rub on — never into the face or on windy sand. A lotion or stick is the better buy.

guides.name: Bug Repellents
guides.descriptionText: Match the active to the bite you actually face. Picaridin or DEET on skin, permethrin on clothes for ticks. Citronella and “natural” oils fade too fast to count on where disease is a risk.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Read the EPA-registered active, not the outdoor lifestyle photo. For mosquitoes on skin, CDC-backed options are picaridin, DEET, IR3535, and oil of lemon eucalyptus (PMD).
Picaridin at about 20% lasts hours, smells less than DEET, and does not melt watch crystals or synthetic gear. It is the usual better everyday skin spray.
DEET works. 20–30% is enough for most days; 100% is not much longer protection and is harsher on skin and plastics. Fine when disease risk is high and that is what you have.
Ticks and brush: treat clothing and shoes with permethrin (or buy pretreated). Never put permethrin on skin. Keep wet spray away from cats and water. Pair with a tick check.
Oil of lemon eucalyptus / PMD is plant-derived and CDC-listed for mosquitoes. Not for children under three. Reapply more often than picaridin.
Citronella, peppermint, lavender, and other essential-oil mists evaporate fast. Backyard comfort at best — not Lyme or dengue protection.
Sunscreen and repellent are two jobs. Put mineral sunscreen on first, wait, then repellent. Combo bottles under-apply both.
Pump spray or lotion on skin; avoid a cloud of aerosol. Reapply after swimming and heavy sweat.
Screens, long sleeves, and pulling ticks off promptly still beat any bottle.
guides.whatMattersMost: A proven active at a useful concentration, used the right way: picaridin or DEET on skin, permethrin on fabric, not a fragrance oil.
guides.commonPitfalls: Citronella as your Lyme plan. Permethrin on skin or around cats. 100% DEET for a patio dinner. A sunscreen–repellent combo. Ultrasonic clips and vitamin B.

keyTypes.name: Picaridin
keyTypes.descriptionText: The best everyday skin repellent for mosquitoes. About 20% lasts several hours, with less odor and less damage to plastics than DEET. CDC-backed. Pump or lotion, not a huge aerosol cloud. Reapply after swimming. Pair with permethrin clothes if ticks are the problem.

keyTypes.name: Permethrin on Clothing
keyTypes.descriptionText: A fabric treatment, not a skin lotion. Kills and repels ticks and mosquitoes that land on pants, shirts, and shoes — the woods and Lyme tool. Buy pretreated gear or spray clothes outdoors, let them dry, and it survives several washes. Never apply to skin. Highly toxic to cats and to aquatic life while wet.

keyTypes.name: DEET
keyTypes.descriptionText: The long-proven mosquito and tick skin repellent. 20–30% covers most outings; higher percentages last only a bit longer and irritate more. Melts some plastics and watch crystals. Fine when disease risk is real and you will reapply. Not kinder to waterways than picaridin, and harsher to live with.

keyTypes.name: Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plant-derived PMD, CDC-listed for mosquitoes at the right concentration (often about 30%). Lasts shorter than picaridin or DEET. Not for children under three. A reasonable “botanical” choice that still has a real active — unlike citronella mist. Check the label for OLE or PMD, not just eucalyptus scent.

keyTypes.name: Citronella & Essential Oils
keyTypes.descriptionText: Citronella, peppermint, lavender, and similar oils smell like protection and evaporate in minutes. Weak against disease mosquitoes and ticks. Candles and wristbands do even less. Fine as a backyard scent if bites are only a nuisance — not a Lyme, dengue, or travel plan.

keyTypes.name: Sunscreen–Repellent Combo
keyTypes.descriptionText: Two jobs on two schedules in one bottle. You need sunscreen more often, and enough of it; DEET or picaridin less often. Combos tend to under-apply both and can reduce SPF. Put sunscreen on first, wait, then a separate repellent. See the Sunscreens guide for zinc.

guides.name: Cancer-Linked Chemicals
guides.descriptionText: Dose and habit beat a scary label. Tobacco, radon, alcohol, and UV cause far more cancer in the U.S. than most grocery or cosmetic warnings. This is not medical advice — it is a shopping and home-habits ranking.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Fix the big four first: do not smoke or vape nicotine, keep the house smoke-free, test for radon, drink less or not at all, and skip tanning beds. Shade, a hat, and mineral sunscreen cover the UV you cannot avoid — see Sunscreens.
California Prop 65 “cancer” stickers appear on everything from coffee to hardware. They are legal warnings, not a ranked risk list. Read them; do not shop by the yellow triangle alone.
Processed meat (bacon, hot dogs, many deli meats) is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen. You do not need to panic over a ballpark frank. Make it rare, not breakfast. Do not char meat to leather; burnt crust is the extra hit.
Eat plants. Washing produce under running water knocks off a lot of residue. Skipping vegetables because of pesticides is the worse cancer trade. Organic or local helps some items; variety and washing help more. See Produce.
PFAS (“forever chemicals”) show up in some nonstick pans, stain-guarded fabrics, and old food wrappers. Stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel skip that coating. Replace a pan when the surface is flaking — do not scour a wrecked PTFE pan into your food.
Formaldehyde off-gasses from some particleboard, laminate, and permanent-press fabric. Air new furniture, prefer used or solid wood, and crack a window. A new dresser in a sealed bedroom is the avoidable case.
Simple cleaners (soap, vinegar, oxygen bleach) plus ventilation beat a cocktail of solvents. See Household Cleaners. Do not mix bleach and ammonia.
Yard fertilizer, weed killers, and insecticides are a separate decision — see Lawn Care.
Old houses: test radon (a cheap short-term kit). Leave suspected asbestos and lead paint to pros — sanding popcorn ceilings and old windows is how those fibers and dust get into you.
Workplace solvents, welding fume, and diesel exhaust can dwarf home products. Follow the job’s ventilation and PPE; that is not a lifestyle brand problem.
guides.whatMattersMost: Tobacco, radon, alcohol, and UV first. Then processed meat, PFAS cookware, and formaldehyde in tight indoor air. Trace labels on shampoo are a distant fifth.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating Prop 65 as a shopping list. Skipping vegetables over pesticide fear. Replacing a working stainless pan with ceramic-nonstick marketing. DIY-sanding old ceilings. Using a vape as a cancer plan.

keyTypes.name: Smoke-Free Living
keyTypes.descriptionText: The highest-leverage cancer move in this guide. Do not smoke cigarettes, and do not treat vapes as a safe substitute for cancer risk. Keep the home and car smoke-free so kids and partners are not breathing it. Ask a clinician for quit help — that beats a new air purifier while someone still smokes inside.

keyTypes.name: Radon Test & Mitigation
keyTypes.descriptionText: Radon is a radioactive gas from soil, the leading cause of lung cancer in U.S. nonsmokers. You cannot smell it. A short-term kit is cheap; if the average is high, a mitigation fan is a real fix. Test the lowest lived-in floor. Smoking plus radon is much worse than either alone.

keyTypes.name: Regular Alcohol Use
keyTypes.descriptionText: Ethanol is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen — mouth, throat, liver, breast, and colon among others. Risk rises with how much and how often, including “moderate” drinking. There is no cancer-safe red wine. Dry days and smaller pours are the practical cut. This is not a moral ranking; it is dose.

keyTypes.name: Processed & Charred Meat
keyTypes.descriptionText: Bacon, hot dogs, ham, and many deli meats are Group 1 for colorectal cancer when they are a habit. Charring steaks and burgers adds extra compounds from the smoke and crust. An occasional cookout is not the same as daily processed meat. Beans, fish, and unburnt poultry are the easier swap — see Everyday Protein.

keyTypes.name: Tanning Beds & Unprotected UV
keyTypes.descriptionText: Solar UV and tanning lamps cause skin cancer, including melanoma. A base tan is not protection. Shade, clothing, and enough mineral sunscreen on leftover skin are the plan — see Sunscreens. Skip the salon bed entirely.

keyTypes.name: PFAS Nonstick Cookware
keyTypes.descriptionText: Older and many cheap nonstick coatings are PTFE/PFAS families that last in people and water. A intact pan used gently is not an emergency; a flaking pan on high heat is the bad case. Skip stain-guard sprays on couches and “performance” food wrappers when you have a choice. Replace worn nonstick; do not sand it.

keyTypes.name: Stainless, Cast Iron & Carbon Steel
keyTypes.descriptionText: No PFAS coating to wear off. Lasts decades if you dry stainless and season iron. The cancer-and-chemical win is skipping recoated nonstick every few years, not a mystical mineral from the skillet. One set you keep beats a ceramic-nonstick marketing cycle.

keyTypes.name: Formaldehyde Pressed Wood
keyTypes.descriptionText: Particleboard, MDF, and some laminates can off-gas formaldehyde, especially when new and in a small closed room. Formaldehyde is a known carcinogen at occupational levels; home air is lower, but ventilation still matters. Prefer used furniture already aired out, solid wood, or lowest-emitting labels. Unpack and air new pieces before they live in a bedroom.

guides.name: Lawn Care
guides.descriptionText: A thick lawn is mowing, watering, and soil — not a monthly chemical calendar. Fertilizer runoff, weed-and-feed, and broadcast insecticides are the usual overkill. Test the soil before you buy a bag.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Soil-test before fertilizer. Many U.S. lawns already have enough phosphorus; extra P is banned for turf in some states because it feeds algae, not grass. If you fertilize, use a slow-release nitrogen in the growing season, not a dump of cheap quick-release before rain.
Leave clippings. They are free nitrogen. Mow high (about 3–3.5 inches for most cool-season grass). Tall grass shades weeds and needs less water.
Water deeply and rarely — about an inch a week, morning — not a daily sprinkle that trains shallow roots.
Overseed thin spots. Clover in the lawn fixes nitrogen; it is not a failure. A mixed green yard beats a sterile monoculture that only lives on product.
Skip weed-and-feed. It spreads herbicide on the whole lawn whether weeds are there or not, and it times fertilizer to the herbicide, not to the grass.
Pull or spot-treat weeds. A ready-to-use 2,4-D or glyphosate dab on a thistle is a different decision from fogging the yard. Keep pets and kids off until the label’s wait is over. Do not spray on a windy day or before a storm.
Broadcast grub and mosquito lawn insecticides, especially neonics, hit bees, aquatic life, and more than the target bug. Tolerate some grub damage, use beneficial nematodes if you must, and skip the spring “insect control” granule as a habit.
The bigger win is less lawn: native groundcover, trees, and a smaller mowable patch cut fertilizer, water, and noise together.
guides.whatMattersMost: Mow high, water deep, feed only what a soil test asks for. Spot weeds; do not subscribe to weed-and-feed or a yearly insecticide.
guides.commonPitfalls: Fertilizing before rain. Phosphorus “for green” when the soil is already loaded. Weed-and-feed as spring tradition. Treating the whole lawn for two dandelions. Neonic granules “just in case.”

keyTypes.name: Mow High, Water Deep, Overseed
keyTypes.descriptionText: The best “product” is a practice. Tall grass crowds weeds, deep watering builds roots, clippings return nitrogen, and overseeding fills bare soil so weeds cannot. No bag, no runoff, no wait-for-pets label. Do this before you buy fertilizer or killer.

keyTypes.name: Compost & Slow-Release Fertilizer
keyTypes.descriptionText: After a soil test, feed what is missing. Compost and slow-release organic or polymer-coated nitrogen leak less to creeks than cheap quick-release. Skip extra phosphorus if the test does not call for it. One modest spring or fall feeding beats a monthly green-up.

keyTypes.name: Quick-Release Synthetic Fertilizer
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cheap nitrogen that greens fast, then burns, then washes into storm drains if rain follows. Feeds algae, not just turf. Fine as a rare rescue on a starved lawn if you water it in and stay off the sidewalk. A poor default every month.

keyTypes.name: Weed-and-Feed Combos
keyTypes.descriptionText: Herbicide plus fertilizer on every square foot, timed to the bag not the weeds. 2,4-D and friends move with runoff and drift onto gardens, pets, and play. You fertilize weeds you do not have and dose grass that may not need nitrogen that week. Spot-treat instead.

keyTypes.name: Spot Weed Treatment
keyTypes.descriptionText: Hand-pull when the soil is wet, or dab a labeled herbicide on a stubborn thistle, poison ivy, or driveway crack. A few milliliters is not a broadcast. Glyphosate and 2,4-D still need PPE, calm wind, and the label’s pet-and-kid wait. Not a weekly ritual — a tool for leftovers after mowing high.

keyTypes.name: Broadcast Weed Killers
keyTypes.descriptionText: Hose-end or granular herbicide on the whole lawn for a uniform look. High volume, high drift and runoff risk, and it selects for weeds that survive. Dandelions in a tall mixed lawn are a taste, not a crisis. If the yard is mostly weeds, overseed and mow high before you buy a bigger bottle.

keyTypes.name: Broadcast Lawn Insecticides
keyTypes.descriptionText: Grub granules, mosquito yard fog, and neonic “insect control” treat the whole turf for bugs you may not have. Neonics and many turf insecticides are hard on bees, aquatic life, and birds that eat treated grubs. Some lawn damage is cheaper than a yearly pesticide. Beneficial nematodes or a targeted product after you confirm grubs is the narrower tool.

guides.name: Cosmetics
guides.descriptionText: “Clean beauty” is unregulated marketing. Shorter formulas, no hidden fragrance, and less product beat a green bottle. PFAS long-wear, plastic glitter, and formaldehyde nail polish are the ones to skip. Face sunscreen is a separate guide.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Read the INCI list, not the front. A short, boring formula you finish is better than a 40-ingredient “clean” stack you dump.
Fragrance / parfum is the biggest blind spot: it can hide dozens of chemicals, including some phthalates and common allergens, without naming them. Unscented or “fragrance-free” (not just “unscented” covering a masker) is the clearer buy for daily face and leave-on lotion.
Paraben-free is not automatically safer. Parabens are well-studied preservatives; some replacements are less tested. Mold in a natural cream is not a health win.
Skip PFAS in long-wear, transfer-proof, and some waterproof mascaras and foundations. If the claim is 24-hour and the list is a mystery fluorinated polymer, pick a wash-off mineral or ordinary formula.
Plastic glitter and old-style microbead scrubs shed into water. Biodegradable cellulose glitter still is not a reason to buy more stuff. Skip rinse-off plastics.
Nail polish: “3-free” or better means no formaldehyde, toluene, or dibutyl phthalate. Formaldehyde keratin treatments are a salon-air problem — ventilate or skip.
Loose talc powder has a history of asbestos contamination in some supply chains. Pressed powder or talc-free is the easier everyday pick; do not inhale clouds of any powder, including mineral.
Mica can involve child labor in some mines. Look for brands that trace mica or use synthetic fluorphlogopite if that is a value for you.
Cruelty-free (Leaping Bunny or equivalent) is about animal tests, not ingredients. Vegan is not the same as safer.
Less is the footprint: one moisturizer, one SPF (see Sunscreens), makeup you actually wear. Refills beat a new compact every season.
This is not medical advice. Patch-test new leave-ons. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals for formaldehyde, PFAS, and fragrance in the bigger picture.
guides.whatMattersMost: Fewer products, fragrance-free leave-ons, and no PFAS or plastic glitter. The label “clean” does not rank risk.
guides.commonPitfalls: Swapping parabens for an untested preservative. Buying seven serums. Inhaling loose powder. “Waterproof 24-hour” as a virtue. Essential-oil “natural” as fragrance-free.

keyTypes.name: Simple Fragrance-Free Formulas
keyTypes.descriptionText: Short INCI lists, a named preservative, no parfum. Leave-on lotion, cleanser, and makeup you can finish. Fragrance-free is not the same as a lavender “natural” scent. The health and waste win is boredom plus finishing the tube.

keyTypes.name: Fewer Products & Refills
keyTypes.descriptionText: Most of cosmetics’ footprint is making and packing jars you barely use. One moisturizer, one SPF, makeup you actually wear. Refill pods and pans you empty beat a new compact every palette drop. Decluttering a 12-step routine is an environmental choice.

keyTypes.name: Mineral Makeup
keyTypes.descriptionText: Iron oxides, zinc, and titanium dioxide as color and coverage — simple, often tinted-zinc friendly next to the Sunscreens guide. Prefer pressed over loose so you do not inhale dust. Ask about mica tracing or synthetic mica if labor is a priority. “Mineral” on the box is not a free pass for added fragrance or PFAS.

keyTypes.name: Undisclosed Fragrance
keyTypes.descriptionText: Parfum, fragrance, or “aroma” can legally hide a mixture, including sensitizers and some phthalates, on daily leave-on skin.
