Prestige scent is the point of many lines — and the least transparent part of the label. If you want smell, a named essential oil is still an allergen; it is not automatically safer. Skip fragrance in products that sit on your face all day.

keyTypes.name: PFAS Long-Wear Makeup
keyTypes.descriptionText: Transfer-proof foundation, some waterproof mascaras, and stain-guard claims can rely on fluorinated (PFAS) film formers. They last in people and water. A formula that washes off with normal cleanser is the easier daily wear. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals for PFAS in the wider home.

keyTypes.name: Plastic Glitter & Microbeads
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plastic glitter and old polyethylene scrub beads become microplastics in water. U.S. rinse-off microbeads are largely banned; glitter, shimmer, and some “peel” products still shed plastic. Cellulose glitter is better but still waste. Skip sparkle you will wash down a sink.

keyTypes.name: Formaldehyde Nail Polish
keyTypes.descriptionText: Older polishes and some keratin/smoothing treatments use formaldehyde, toluene, or dibutyl phthalate. Indoor air plus fingertips is the exposure. Buy 3-free or better polish, cap the bottle, and ventilate salon treatments. Formaldehyde is a known carcinogen at high occupational levels — see Cancer-Linked Chemicals. A basic 3-free polish is the ordinary swap.

guides.name: Laundry
guides.descriptionText: Most of the impact is heat, not the brand of soap. Wash cold, fill the machine, skip scent beads, and dry on a line or a rack when you can. A vented dryer on every load is the expensive habit.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Wash cold. Modern detergents are built for it. Hot water is for true sanitation — illness, or a cloth-diaper pail that sat (see Diapers) — not Tuesday T-shirts and not every diaper load. Heating the water is most of a cycle’s energy.
Full loads, measured soap. More detergent does not clean more; it leaves residue and needs extra rinses. HE machines need a small dose. Powder or a concentrate in cardboard beats a parade of bottles.
Fragrance-free. Scent beads, “odor” boosters, and heavy perfume in detergent are leave-on chemicals in your clothes and indoor air. They do not clean. Softener and dryer sheets coat fibers — towels stay less absorbent, synthetics shed a bit easier to wash out.
Skip pods if you can. Convenient, easy to overdose on a small load, a poisoning risk for kids, and a plastic film plus a locked-in formula. Liquid or powder you dose is the clearer buy.
Dry without a fire. Line, rack, or a spin-heavy cycle then air. A heat-pump dryer uses a fraction of a conventional vented dryer if you need a machine (apartments, pollen, winter). Clean the lint trap; over-drying wastes energy and wears clothes.
Synthetics shed microplastics. Wash less often, use a catch bag or in-machine filter, skip fabric softener, and prefer a full cold load to many half-hot ones. See Clothing for the fiber itself.
The machine matters less than the settings until you replace it. When you do, a heat-pump dryer and a cold-capable washer beat a scented “eco” bottle on a hot vented stack.
guides.whatMattersMost: Cold water, full loads, no scent beads, and air-dry or a heat-pump dryer. The detergent brand is a distant second.
guides.commonPitfalls: Hot wash “to get it really clean.” Scent beads as hygiene. Half loads with a pod. Dryer sheets on towels. Replacing a working washer to fix a hot-water habit.

keyTypes.name: Cold Wash & Air Dry
keyTypes.descriptionText: The highest-leverage laundry habit. Cold water skips the heater; a line, rack, or extra spin then air skips the dryer. Clothes last longer. Works for almost everything except true sanitizing loads. Do this before you buy a new machine or a greener bottle.

keyTypes.name: Fragrance-Free Detergent
keyTypes.descriptionText: Powder or concentrated liquid, dose for a full HE load, no perfume, no beads. Cleaning enzymes do the work. Cardboard or a refill beats a new bottle every month. “Free and clear” still check the label — some add a masking scent. This is the soap, not a substitute for cold water.

keyTypes.name: Heat-Pump Dryer
keyTypes.descriptionText: When you cannot line-dry — weather, pollen, a closed apartment — a heat-pump dryer recycles heat and uses much less electricity than a conventional vented dryer. Slower, gentler on clothes, no exterior vent. Only worth buying when the old dryer dies; settings on the current machine still matter more this year.

keyTypes.name: Laundry Pods
keyTypes.descriptionText: Pre-dosed and easy to overuse on a small load. PVA film plus a locked scent-and-surfactant mix. A real poisoning hazard if a child treats them like candy. Fine as an occasional travel hack; a poor default compared with powder you measure. They do not make hot water optional.

keyTypes.name: Scent Beads & Dryer Sheets
keyTypes.descriptionText: They do not clean. Beads add perfume and extra plastic-adjacent chemistry to a load that already has detergent. Sheets coat fabric, cut towel absorbency, and can gum up dryer sensors. Indoor air plus skin contact for hours. Skip them. Wool balls or nothing if you need static control.

keyTypes.name: Hot Wash & Vented Dryer
keyTypes.descriptionText: The default American stack: hot cycle, extra rinse, then a long vented dry until everything is stiff. Most of household laundry energy lives here. Harder on clothes, higher bills, more microfiber break-up. Save a hot cycle for illness, a diaper pail that sat (everyday cloth is a warm full load — see Diapers), or oily shop towels — not every load of jeans.

guides.name: Gas vs Induction
guides.descriptionText: A gas burner is a combustion appliance in the kitchen: nitrogen dioxide, some carbon monoxide, and methane leaks even when the knob is off. Induction heats the pan, not the air, and skips the flame. Vent the hood if you keep gas until you switch.
guides.buyingAdvice:
If the range is dying, induction is the usual better buy: faster boil, easier simmer, no combustion indoors, and higher efficiency than a coil or a flame. You need a magnetic pan (a magnet sticks to the bottom) — cast iron and many stainless pans already work. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals for skipping PFAS nonstick while you are at it.
Gas is not “just like grandma.” Unburned methane leaks from stoves and pipes; the flame makes NO₂. That is an indoor-air problem, especially in small kitchens and with kids in the house. A window is not a range hood.
If you keep gas for now: a hood that vents outdoors, on high, covering the front burners, every time you cook. Recirculating “hoods” that only filter grease do not dump NO₂ outside. Simmer with a lid. Never use the stove or oven as a heater.
Electric coil or smooth-top resistance is cleaner indoor air than gas but slower and less efficient than induction. A fine bridge if wiring or budget blocks induction this year.
The swap cost is often the 240-volt circuit, not the cooktop. Portable single-burner induction on a regular outlet is a real trial and a useful extra burner. “Renewable gas” and hydrogen-ready stickers do not fix indoor combustion this decade.
This is not medical advice. If anyone has asthma, take kitchen air seriously and talk with a clinician about the home.
guides.whatMattersMost: No flame in the kitchen when you can help it. Induction first; a venting hood if you still cook on gas.
guides.commonPitfalls: A recirculating microwave hood as ventilation. Buying aluminum pans that will not couple to induction. Using the oven to heat the house. Waiting for hydrogen in the pipe.
guides.searchTerms: induction,gas stove,cooktop,range,NO2,methane,electric stove,range hood,induction hob,natural gas,cooking

keyTypes.name: Induction Cooktop
keyTypes.descriptionText: The pan is the heater. No combustion, little wasted heat, fast boil, precise simmer. Needs magnetic cookware and usually a 240-volt circuit for a full range; a portable burner can test the idea on a regular outlet. Pairs with stainless and cast iron you keep for decades. Cleaner indoor air than gas on any grid mix; cleaner climate as the grid gets greener.

keyTypes.name: Electric Coil or Smooth-Top
keyTypes.descriptionText: No indoor flame, so no cooking NO₂ from the burner. Slower and less efficient than induction: the element heats, then the pan. A fair bridge if you already have 240-volt electric and cannot do induction yet. Still beats unvented gas for household air.

keyTypes.name: Gas Range with Vented Hood
keyTypes.descriptionText: Keep gas only if a hood actually dumps air outdoors, you run it on high while cooking, and you are not using the stove as heat. Cuts some NO₂; it does not stop methane leaks from the appliance or the pipe. A holding pattern until induction, not a climate strategy. Recirculating hoods do not qualify.

keyTypes.name: Unvented Gas Cooking
keyTypes.descriptionText: A gas cooktop or oven with no outdoor-venting hood — or a hood you never turn on. Indoor NO₂, moisture, and particles stay in the living space. Methane still leaks when the burner is off. The common U.S. setup, and the one to change first: vent, then replace with induction when the appliance turns over.

guides.name: Refrigerators
guides.descriptionText: A fridge runs every hour for a decade. Size, ice makers, and whether you keep a second one in the garage usually beat the brand name. Manufacturing is heavy — do not junk a healthy five-year-old box for a sticker.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep a working fridge. Clean the coils, check the door gasket, keep it 37–40°F and the freezer at 0°F, and give it space to vent. Repair is the climate win until the compressor is dead or the unit is a 15–20 year energy hog.
When you replace: buy the smallest box that holds a week of real food. Top-freezer Energy Star models use less electricity than French-door and side-by-side theater kitchens. Through-door ice and water are convenient leaks — extra energy, extra repairs.
Prefer a hydrocarbon refrigerant (R-600a / isobutane) over older high-GWP HFCs when the spec sheet lists it. Have the old unit hauled by a program that recovers refrigerant — do not vent it in the driveway.
One fridge. A second garage unit that holds condiments and beer can use as much as the kitchen fridge. If you must, fill it, set it warmer, and retire it when you can.
Do not upsize “for entertaining.” An emptier, larger cavity still runs. See Home Electricity for the power behind the plug, and Laundry for the same keep-vs-replace logic on dryers.
guides.whatMattersMost: One right-sized, efficient box you keep for years. A second fridge and a giant ice-dispenser door are the usual waste.
guides.commonPitfalls: Replacing a six-year-old fridge for Energy Star. An empty garage freezer on high. Setting the kitchen unit colder than 37°F. Skipping refrigerant recovery at disposal.
guides.searchTerms: refrigerator,fridge,freezer,energy star,R-600a,ice maker,garage fridge,appliance,side by side,french door

keyTypes.name: Keep, Repair & Maintain
keyTypes.descriptionText: The best fridge is the one already in the kitchen, if the seals and compressor still work. Coils, gaskets, and sane temperatures save more this year than a new manufacture cycle. Replace when it is truly old and inefficient or when repair costs more than a decade of extra kWh — not because a showroom is on sale.

keyTypes.name: Energy Star Top-Freezer
keyTypes.descriptionText: When you do buy: right-sized, top freezer, Energy Star, hydrocarbon refrigerant if listed. Fewest gizmos, lowest typical kWh, longest-proven layout. Ugly and cheap compared with a French door — and that is the point. Recycle the old unit properly.

keyTypes.name: Energy Star French Door
keyTypes.descriptionText: Bottom freezer, wide fresh-food access, more gasket and more lights. Energy Star still helps. Fine if the household actually fills it and you skip the ice-through-the-door option. A larger cavity than you need cancels the efficiency label. Acceptable when a top-freezer will not fit how you cook.

keyTypes.name: Side-by-Side with Ice Dispenser
keyTypes.descriptionText: Tall doors, through-door ice and water, extra fans and heaters against sweat. Convenient, leak-prone, and typically hungrier than a top-freezer of the same volume. Buy only if accessibility needs a side-by-side — not as the default upgrade.

keyTypes.name: Second Garage Fridge
keyTypes.descriptionText: The silent load: a spare refrigerator or freezer in the garage or basement, often an old kitchen hand-me-down, half empty, fighting heat. Can match the kitchen fridge’s yearly electricity. Fill it or unplug it. A cooler with ice for a party is cheaper than a permanent second box.

guides.name: Furniture
guides.descriptionText: The climate and chemical cost is making a new piece, then throwing it out in five years. Used and solid wood you keep beat particleboard that off-gasses in a closed bedroom. Formaldehyde is covered in more depth under Cancer-Linked Chemicals.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Use what you have. Tighten joints, re-glue, recover a sound frame. A repaired dresser is the lowest-impact furniture there is.
Buy used next: thrift, estate, marketplace, office surplus. It has already off-gassed, and you skip a manufacture cycle. Inspect joints, rust, and pests — not the finish fashion.
New: solid wood or plywood with a known mill (FSC or equivalent) lasts decades if you will actually keep it. Tropical hardwoods need a real chain of custody, not a “mango wood” vibe.
Composite (particleboard, MDF) is fine for cheap, short-stay pieces if it meets current U.S. formaldehyde limits (TSCA Title VI / CARB Phase 2) and you air it before a bedroom. Unlabeled fast-furniture board in a sealed room is the avoidable case.
Upholstery: a sturdy used frame plus new fabric beats a foam-and-staple sofa every few years. Skip PVC “leather.” Flame-retardant foam is a health and disposal headache — look for furniture that meets smolder standards without additive soup when you can.
Do not buy a matching seven-piece set you will leave at the curb. One table you like for twenty years is the ethical and climate win.
guides.whatMattersMost: Years of use. Used or solid wood you keep; not a particleboard bedroom set on a three-year cycle.
guides.commonPitfalls: A new “eco” composite set every move. Unlabeled board in a nursery. PVC leather. Tropical hardwood with no paperwork. Skipping Cancer-Linked Chemicals for the formaldehyde detail.

keyTypes.name: Used Furniture & Repair
keyTypes.descriptionText: The best piece is already in the house or at the thrift store. Repair, refinish, recover. Off-gassing is mostly done. Labor and forest impact already happened. Inspect structure, not Instagram finish. This is the same keep-it logic as phones and fridges.

keyTypes.name: Solid Wood Furniture
keyTypes.descriptionText: New or new-to-you hardwood/plywood built to last, with FSC or a mill you can name. Repairable joints, not cam locks in crumbling board. Worth the money only if you will keep it through moves. Skip mystery tropical boards without a custody claim.

keyTypes.name: Low-Emitting Composite Furniture
keyTypes.descriptionText: Particleboard or MDF that meets current U.S. formaldehyde limits (TSCA Title VI / CARB Phase 2), aired out before a bedroom. Fine for a short-stay desk or a rental you will not keep forever. Still a short life versus solid wood. Not a license for a whole matching suite every five years.

keyTypes.name: Fast-Furniture Particleboard
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cam-lock, paper veneer, unlabeled board, designed to fail at the next move. High formaldehyde risk when new and sealed in a small room — see Cancer-Linked Chemicals. Forest and labor are opaque. The curb pile in three years is the real product. Used or one solid piece costs less over a decade.

keyTypes.name: PVC Faux-Leather Upholstery
keyTypes.descriptionText: Vinyl “leather” on foam frames: plasticizers, a short crack-and-peel life, and a sofa you cannot repair. Real leather has cattle impacts (see Shoes). A used cloth or leather frame you recover is the better sitting surface. Skip the showroom vinyl sectional.

guides.name: Laptops & Computers
guides.descriptionText: Most of a computer’s footprint is mining and manufacturing, same as a phone. Keeping it, then buying refurbished, beats a new thin-and-light every three years. Repairable machines and extra RAM/SSD are the climate features.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep the one you have. A RAM or SSD upgrade and a fresh battery often add years. OS updates ending is annoying; it is not a reason to landfill a working motherboard. See Smartphones for the same manufacturing-first logic.
Refurbished or certified used is the usual next buy. Business laptops (replaceable storage, documented batteries) last. Check keyboard, ports, and battery cycle count.
If you buy new: pick something you can open — replaceable storage at least, published parts, long software support. A modular or classic serviceable laptop costs more up front and less per year. Avoid glued-shut fashion ultrabooks you will toss when the battery dies.
Desktops are easier to repair and cool; a used tower plus a kept monitor is a strong stationary setup. Gaming PCs that turn over with every GPU generation are a hobby tax, not a need.
School Chromebooks that die in two years are a volume problem. Buy the unit you can still use after the class ends, or a used ThinkPad-class machine.
Recycle through a certified e-waste program. Hard-drive wipe first. Do not throw boards in household trash.
The efficient charger and a laptop you use for eight years beat a new “ENERGY STAR” chassis you replace in three.
guides.whatMattersMost: Years in service. Keep and repair, then refurbished. A sealed new laptop on a three-year cycle is the expensive habit.
guides.commonPitfalls: A new ultrabook because the old one feels slow — try RAM/SSD first. Chromebooks you cannot keep. GPU upgrades as identity. Skipping a wipe before recycling.

keyTypes.name: Keep & Repair Computer
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact machine is already on the desk. Add RAM or an SSD, replace a battery, clean fans, and keep the monitor. Software support ending does not make the aluminum and chips disappear. Same rule as a phone: manufacturing dominates.

keyTypes.name: Refurbished Laptop
keyTypes.descriptionText: Certified used or business off-lease: the mining already happened, the price is lower, and the chassis is often more serviceable than a new consumer slim. Inspect battery health and ports. A strong next step when keep-and-repair is no longer enough.

keyTypes.name: New Repairable Laptop
keyTypes.descriptionText: When you need new: user-replaceable storage, published spare parts, and years of OS updates. Heavier, uglier, and more honest than a sealed wedge. Only pays off if you keep it a long time. Framework-style modular or classic serviceable business laptops are the type, not a brand religion.

keyTypes.name: Sealed Thin-and-Light Laptop
keyTypes.descriptionText: Glued battery, soldered RAM, fashion chassis. Fine in the backpack for a year; costly when the battery swells or storage fills. The three-year upgrade loop is how computers rival cars in embodied carbon per household. Refurbished or repairable is the better default.

keyTypes.name: Gaming PC Upgrade Cycle
keyTypes.descriptionText: A desktop you rebuild every GPU generation: high power draw, high manufacturing, short pride of ownership. A used tower you actually finish games on is a hobby. A new top-chip every launch is not. Keep the case and PSU; buy GPUs used; do not treat 4K max settings as a climate-neutral need.

guides.name: Toilet Paper & Paper Towels
guides.descriptionText: This is a forest product you flush or trash after one use. Using less — a bidet, cloth rags, recycled rolls — beats a “softer” virgin sheet from old trees. Bamboo is a tree-free virgin fiber, not a free pass.
guides.buyingAdvice:
The win is fewer sheets, not a greener brand of the same habit. A bidet seat or a cheap non-electric attachment cuts toilet paper sharply. You may still want a little paper to dry. Water per rinse is small next to growing, pulping, bleaching, wrapping, and trucking a roll.
Kitchen: washable rags and cloth napkins for counters, hands, and spills. Keep a short stack of paper towels for raw-meat juice or a truly filthy mess if that is your hygiene line — not for every drip. Wash cloth with a regular cold load (see Laundry); do not run a hot cycle for two rags.
When you buy paper: 100% recycled, preferably post-consumer, processed chlorine-free (PCF). Recycled uses waste that already exists. Ultra-plush “quilted” tissue is usually virgin pulp, often from northern and boreal forests that store a lot of carbon, for a product that lasts seconds.
Unbleached or PCF recycled is the cleaner bleach story. Old chlorine bleaching made dioxins; modern elemental-chlorine-free (ECF) virgin mills are better than that era, and still not a reason to pick virgin over recycled.
Bamboo toilet paper is tree-free virgin fiber. Bamboo grows fast. It is still a new harvest, often pulped and shipped a long way, and sometimes mixed with wood. Prefer it to boreal plush if recycled is not on the shelf — not as a swap for using less, and not as automatically greener than recycled office paper.
Skip “flushable” wipes. Many contain plastic, clog pipes, and do not belong in a septic tank. If you need a wipe, a wet washcloth you launder is the version that does not become a fatberg.
Septic systems like ordinary TP that breaks up; they do not like wipes, “septic-safe” marketing on rock-hard virgin rolls, or paper towels down the bowl.
Buying in bulk cardboard with no extra plastic wrap beats individually wrapped mega-rolls of virgin plush. The climate feature is still the bidet and the rag drawer.
guides.whatMattersMost: Use less. Bidet and cloth first; recycled PCF paper when you need a roll. Virgin ultra-soft and a paper-towel habit are the forest cost.
guides.commonPitfalls: Bamboo as a climate trophy while you still use a roll a week. “Flushable” wipes. Quilted virgin TP for softness. Paper towels as the default kitchen cloth. Pretending recycled is too scratchy to try.

keyTypes.name: Bidet & Less Paper
keyTypes.descriptionText: A bidet seat or a non-electric attachment is the big cut in toilet-paper volume. Manufacture once, use for years. You may still keep a recycled roll to dry. Water per rinse is tiny next to pulping trees. Check toilet fit and a GFCI outlet if you go electric. Not a medical device — skip it if a clinician has told you otherwise.

keyTypes.name: Cloth Rags & Napkins
keyTypes.descriptionText: The paper-towel replacement: worn towels cut into rags, a sponge, cloth napkins. Wash with a regular cold load. Keep a few paper sheets for raw meat or biohazard if you want that line. The climate cost of cloth is laundry — do not add a hot extra cycle for two rags.

keyTypes.name: Recycled Chlorine-Free Tissue
keyTypes.descriptionText: Toilet paper or towels from recycled fiber, ideally post-consumer and processed chlorine-free. Uses paper that already exists instead of pulp from standing forests. Can feel less plush — that is the point of not milling old trees for a flush. The right roll when a bidet or rag is not enough.

keyTypes.name: Bamboo Virgin Tissue
keyTypes.descriptionText: Tree-free, but still a virgin harvest: bamboo pulp, often shipped far, sometimes blended with wood. Faster-growing than boreal spruce, not automatically better than recycled paper sitting in a sorting plant. A reasonable shelf pick versus ultra-plush virgin wood — not a reason to skip the bidet or to treat “bamboo” as a climate offset.

keyTypes.name: Virgin Plush Toilet Paper
keyTypes.descriptionText: Quilted, extra-soft, extra-strong rolls from virgin wood — often northern and boreal forest pulp — used for seconds and flushed. High carbon store in, high waste out. “Septic-safe” on the package does not fix the forest. Recycled or less paper is the actual upgrade.

keyTypes.name: Disposable Paper-Towel Habit
keyTypes.descriptionText: A roll on every spill, plus “flushable” wipes that are often plastic and a plumber’s problem. Same forest and mill cost as plush TP, then a trash bag. Cloth rags cover most kitchen jobs. Wipes do not belong in the toilet, septic or sewer.

guides.name: Pet Food
guides.descriptionText: Many households feed more animal product to pets than they eat themselves. Meat volume is the climate cost — especially beef, lamb, and “human-grade” steaks for a dog. Cats need meat; dogs are more flexible. This is not a reason to rehome a living animal.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep the pet you have. The climate decision is the bowl, not a guilt trip about an animal already in the house. Do not add a second large dog as a lifestyle accessory. Overfeeding is extra livestock for fat pets — measure, and skip the extra cheese.
Poultry-based complete food that uses animal byproducts is the usual better buy. Rendering leftover chicken into kibble or cans feeds a pet on parts people already declined. “Human-grade,” “fresh,” and “real steak in every bowl” often means extra animals raised for pets, which is the opposite of efficient.
Dogs can do well on a complete, AAFCO- or WSAVA-style formulated diet with less ruminant meat, including some veterinary plant-inclusive or insect-protein foods. That is a nutrition formula, not DIY rice and beans. Talk to a veterinarian before you switch, especially for puppies, seniors, and sick dogs.
Cats are obligate carnivores. They need preformed taurine and other nutrients from animal tissue. Do not put a cat on a homemade or vegan diet to save the climate. Ordinary complete poultry cat food, portioned, is the honest path. Boutique fish and tuna-every-meal has the same stock problems as people food — see Seafood.
Skip beef, lamb, and venison as the everyday protein unless a vet wants a novel protein for a true allergy. Same methane logic as Everyday Protein.
Raw and freeze-dried “prey” diets do not have good evidence they are healthier, and they can spread Salmonella in the kitchen. They are also a lot of extra high-grade meat.
Grain-free is a marketing era, not a climate or health upgrade. Treats, chews, and table scraps are a second bowl — count them.
This is not veterinary advice. If your pet has a medical diet, follow the clinician, not a footprint chart.
guides.whatMattersMost: Less meat, especially less beef, in a complete food you actually measure. Byproduct poultry beats a fresh-steak subscription. Cats still need meat.
guides.commonPitfalls: Human-grade as kindness. A second helping as love. Vegan cats. Raw as ancestral. Grain-free as greener. Rehoming a healthy pet to fix a climate spreadsheet.

keyTypes.name: Measured Poultry Pet Food
keyTypes.descriptionText: Complete kibble or cans based on chicken or turkey, including byproducts — the parts of animals already slaughtered for people. Portion to the pet’s body, not the bag’s generosity. The default climate-honest bowl for dogs and the right idea for cats, who still need animal tissue. Not a steak, not a second dinner of treats.

keyTypes.name: Vet Lower-Meat Dog Food
keyTypes.descriptionText: A complete, formulated dog food with more plants or less ruminant meat, chosen with a veterinarian — including some commercial plant-inclusive diets that meet AAFCO-style completeness. Dogs are not wolves on a spreadsheet. Puppies, medical cases, and all cats are outside this swap. DIY kitchen scraps are not a diet.

keyTypes.name: Insect Protein Dog Food
keyTypes.descriptionText: Black soldier fly or similar complete dog foods: animal protein with a smaller land footprint than chicken, far smaller than beef. Still a processed diet that must be complete. Supply is limited, cats are not automatically included, and “bugs” are not a reason to skip portions. A solid Acceptable when the bag is truly formulated for dogs.

keyTypes.name: Human-Grade Fresh Pet Meat
keyTypes.descriptionText: Subscription packs of lightly cooked “people food” for pets: extra livestock, extra refrigeration, extra price. Kindness-shaped marketing that often uses more chicken breast and beef than a byproduct kibble. If a vet prescribes a fresh diet, that is medicine. As a lifestyle default, it is a second meat habit in the house.

keyTypes.name: Beef, Lamb & Raw Pet Diet
keyTypes.descriptionText: Ruminant meat and raw or freeze-dried “prey” bowls. High methane (see Everyday Protein), extra high-grade muscle, and a kitchen Salmonella risk that does not have strong health evidence behind it. Novel-protein beef or venison for a diagnosed allergy is a vet call. Everyday “ancestral” raw is a climate and hygiene miss.

guides.name: Food Storage
guides.descriptionText: The climate win is leftovers you actually eat, not a matching set of new glass. Reuse jars and tubs you have. Buy glass or silicone when plastic is dying. Daily cling wrap and baggies are the expensive habit. “Compostable” bags in a landfill are still trash.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep food. Spoiled produce and leftover takeout dwarf the footprint of a bag (see Produce and Refrigerators). A container you will use beats a prettier one you will not.
Use what is already in the cupboard: jam jars, yogurt tubs, the plastic boxes that still seal. Do not landfill a working lid to buy a glass nested set. Wash and keep.
When you buy: glass or stainless with a lid you can replace. They microwave and fridge without scratching into haze as fast as cheap plastic. Heavy, breakable — not for every lunchbox.
Silicone zip bags are the freezer and sandwich job reusable plastic was supposed to be. Manufacture once, wash for years. They are still a factory product; a drawer of six is plenty.
Beeswax wraps cover cheese, bread, and a bowl. Not raw meat. Wash cool, not hot. They wear out and are not a compost miracle if they have synthetic grit. A few wraps beat a cling-film roll; they do not beat a jar.
Skip the daily zip bag and the box of plastic wrap. One bag reused as a trash liner is different from a new bag for every apple. Foil is energy-intensive to make — reuse a sheet when you can; recycle it clean; do not treat it as green.
“Compostable” and PLA bags usually need an industrial pile you do not have. In the trash they act like plastic. They contaminate recycling. Not a drop-in upgrade.
See Shopping Bags for the grocery-carry version of the same reuse rule. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals if you are swapping old scratched plastic for grease-proof papers that may use PFAS.
guides.whatMattersMost: Eat the leftover. Reuse jars first; glass or silicone when you need a lid. Daily baggies and fake-compost bags are the miss.
guides.commonPitfalls: Tossing decent plastic for a Instagram glass set. Compostable bags in the garbage. Beeswax on raw chicken. A new baggie for every snack. Foil as a climate flex.

keyTypes.name: Reuse Jars & Tubs You Have
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact container is already washed in the rack: pasta sauce jars, yogurt tubs, deli boxes that still seal. Manufacturing already happened. Match the lid, skip buying a set. Food you save in them is the climate feature. Same keep-it logic as a phone or a fridge.

keyTypes.name: Glass or Stainless Food Storage
keyTypes.descriptionText: When you need to buy: a glass or stainless box with a replaceable lid, used for years. Inert in the fridge and microwave, easy to see leftovers, recyclable at end of life. Heavy and breakable. Worth it if you will actually wash it — not as a reason to trash working plastic.

keyTypes.name: Silicone Reusable Bags
keyTypes.descriptionText: Stand-up freezer and lunch bags you wash instead of tossing. Silicone is still manufactured; a small set used hundreds of times beats a box of zip bags a month. Not infinitely “plastic-free” in the factory sense. Do not buy twelve colors. Fine when a jar is the wrong shape.

keyTypes.name: Beeswax Wraps
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cloth plus wax for cheese, bread, and covering a bowl. Cuts cling film for those jobs. Not for raw meat or hot pans. Cool wash only; they crack and go in the trash, not a backyard compost pile, if the fabric is synthetic. A few wraps, not a drawer of novelty prints. Beeswax is an animal product — skip if that is a value for you and use a plate or a jar.

keyTypes.name: Daily Plastic Wrap & Baggies
keyTypes.descriptionText: A new film or zip bag for every sandwich, leftover, and cucumber half. Cheap per box, expensive per year, and a liner in the ocean and the landfill. Reuse a bag until it fails if you still buy them. The wrap habit is the problem, not one bag that saved a stew from the trash.

keyTypes.name: Compostable Storage Bags
keyTypes.descriptionText: PLA and “plant plastic” bags marketed as the drop-in green zip. Most curbside compost will not take them; they do not belong in the recycling bin; in a landfill they do not magically disappear. A reusable jar beats a compostable bag you throw away. Same reuse rule as Shopping Bags.

guides.name: Batteries
guides.descriptionText: Mining and making a cell is the cost; throwing it away after one remote is the habit. Low-self-discharge NiMH in AA/AAA, and keeping the battery already in a phone or laptop, beat a drawer of alkalines. Lithium does not go in household trash.
guides.buyingAdvice:
For AA and AAA in remotes, toys, lights, and controllers: nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) rechargeables with low self-discharge, plus a charger you keep. After a few dozen cycles they beat throwaways on money and mining. Match the size. Do not mix old and new, or NiMH with alkaline, in the same device.
Do not put rechargeables in a smoke or CO alarm unless the maker says so. A dead silent alarm is worse than an alkaline pack the label asked for. Follow the device. Ten-year sealed detectors skip the yearly battery dance.
The pack in a phone, laptop, earbuds, or drill is already the expensive lithium. Keep the device (see Smartphones and Laptops & Computers). A spare power bank is useful if you travel; a drawer of unused banks is extra mining.
Alkaline is fine as a backup, for a clock you open once a year, or where the manual requires it. It is not the weekly toy-aisle default. “Heavy duty” carbon-zinc is weaker still.
Primary lithium (camera CR123, coin cells, some smoke units) holds a lot of energy and is not a NiMH swap. Recycle them as batteries — never the kitchen trash or a fire pit. Coin cells: keep them away from kids; swallowing is an emergency.
Car lead-acid batteries already have a recycling path. Take the old one when you buy the new one. Do not dump acid.
Household alkaline recycling is low-value; the win is not buying the dump in the first place. Lithium, NiMH, NiCad, and lead-acid need a real take-back (store bin, municipal household hazardous waste).
This is not fire-safety or medical advice. Damaged or swollen lithium packs: do not crush; use a battery drop-off.
guides.whatMattersMost: Recharge AA/AAA. Keep the lithium already in your devices. Recycle lithium and button cells; do not trash them.
guides.commonPitfalls: Alkaline for every game controller. NiMH in a smoke alarm the label forbids. A power-bank collection. Coin cells in the junk drawer. Lithium in the kitchen bin.

keyTypes.name: NiMH Rechargeable Cells
keyTypes.descriptionText: Low-self-discharge nickel-metal hydride AA/AAA and a charger you keep. Hundreds of cycles. The default for remotes, toys, headlamps, and controllers. Mining happens once per pack instead of per dump. Not for every smoke alarm — read the label. Do not mix with alkaline in the same gadget.

keyTypes.name: Keep the Device Battery
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lithium pack already in the phone, laptop, earbuds, or drill is the heavy manufacturing. Using it until it fails — then a repair or a certified recycle — beats a new gadget or a stack of idle power banks. Same keep-it logic as Smartphones and Laptops & Computers. A single bank for travel is a tool; a collection is inventory.

keyTypes.name: Occasional Alkaline
keyTypes.descriptionText: A pack of alkaline for the clock, the flashlight in a disaster kit, or a detector that specifies it. Low drain, rare swap. Not a weekly shopping item. Recycle if your town takes them; the climate win is still buying few. Better than lithium primaries for jobs that do not need them.

keyTypes.name: Single-Use Alkaline Habit
keyTypes.descriptionText: A new four-pack for every toy, every party, every dead remote. Zinc and manganese mined, canned, dumped. “Heavy duty” carbon-zinc is the same story with less capacity. Rechargeables pay off fast in anything you use weekly. This habit is the household battery problem.

keyTypes.name: Loose Lithium in the Trash
keyTypes.descriptionText: Coin cells, camera lithium, vape sticks, swollen phone packs, and power banks in the kitchen bin. Fire risk in trucks and at the dump, plus metals that belong in a battery take-back. Primary lithium is sometimes the right chemistry — it is never the right trash. Store coin cells away from children.

guides.name: Dishwashing
guides.descriptionText: A full efficient dishwasher that you scrape, not rinse, uses less water and heat than a running tap. Air-dry. If you have no machine, a basin of wash water then a short rinse beats the faucet left open. The detergent brand is a distant second — same story as Laundry.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Fill the machine. ENERGY STAR dishwashers typically use a few gallons a load — less than washing the same pile under a running tap. Scrape into the compost or trash; skip the pre-rinse. Modern enzyme detergents want food soil. Half loads and “just these mugs” waste the fill.
Skip heated dry. Open the door or use air-dry. A rinse aid can help spots so you do not turn the heater back on. Normal or eco beats pots-and-pans for Tuesday plates.
Soap: a dose of powder or a simple tablet, fragrance-free if indoor air matters to you. Pods are convenient, easy to over-use on a tiny load, and a plastic film plus a kid-poisoning risk — same caution as Laundry pods. Phosphate-free is already the U.S. default; “green” on the box is not a water-saving cycle.
No dishwasher: wash in a pan or stoppered sink, then rinse. Do not leave the tap roaring for twenty minutes. Water heat is the energy cost (see Laundry). A brush and a drainboard beat a new sponge every day.
Keep a working dishwasher. When it dies, an ENERGY STAR unit you fill is the upgrade — not a showroom panel you run half-empty. Hand-washing “to save electricity” while the tap runs is usually the wrong trade.
This is not a sanitation protocol. Illness, baby bottles, and canning jars follow a clinician or a tested method, not a footprint chart.
guides.whatMattersMost: A full scrape-and-run load, air-dry — or a basin if you have no machine. A running tap is the expensive habit.
guides.commonPitfalls: Pre-rinsing every plate. Half loads. Heated dry as a default. Hand-washing with the faucet open “to save the machine.” A scented pod for four cups.
guides.searchTerms: dishwasher,dishwashing,dish soap,pods,hand wash,pre-rinse,ENERGY STAR,air dry,detergent,running water

keyTypes.name: Full Dishwasher, Air Dry
keyTypes.descriptionText: Scrape, load it full, skip pre-rinse, skip heated dry. An efficient dishwasher uses a few gallons and less heat than a sink marathon. The climate feature is the full rack, not the stainless finish. Keep the machine you have until it fails; settings beat a new panel this year.

keyTypes.name: Basin Hand Wash
keyTypes.descriptionText: No dishwasher, or a few pots that cannot go in: a sink or tub of hot soapy water, then a short rinse. Heat the water once. A drainboard dries. This beats an open tap and can rival a half-empty machine. Still more labor; still the right method when the rack is the wrong tool.

keyTypes.name: Fragrance-Free Dish Detergent
keyTypes.descriptionText: Powder or a simple dose for a full load — enzymes clean, perfume does not. Cardboard or a refill beats a pod pyramid. Phosphate-free is already standard in the U.S. This is the soap, not a substitute for filling the rack or turning off the tap. Same fragrance logic as Laundry.

keyTypes.name: Running-Tap Hand Wash
keyTypes.descriptionText: The faucet open while you chat, rinse, and re-rinse. Tens of gallons of heated water for a pile a dishwasher would do in about four. Feels thrifty (“I’m not running the machine”). It is not. A basin, or a full dishwasher, is the actual save.

keyTypes.name: Pre-Rinse, Half Load, Heated Dry
keyTypes.descriptionText: Hose every plate, run a short rack, then bake the dishes dry. You pay for water twice and heat twice. Modern detergent wants the soil; the heater wants your bill. Fill it, scrape it, air-dry. A pod on four mugs is the same overkill as a laundry pod on a handful of shirts.

guides.name: Tires
guides.descriptionText: Tread wear is a major source of microplastics, and most tires still use an antioxidant (6PPD) that has killed coho salmon. You cannot shop that chemical away at the counter yet. Inflate, rotate, and run a tire to a safe end of life so you shed fewer grams and buy fewer sets. Pair with Getting Around for the miles themselves.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Air pressure first. A soft tire wears faster, wastes fuel, and handles worse. Check cold, to the door-jamb number, not the sidewall maximum. Rotate on the schedule in the manual. Alignment when it pulls. That is the climate and particle win before you buy anything.
Replace for safety, not fashion. U.S. passenger tread is done at 2/32 inch — sooner if cords, bulges, or dry rot. Driving bald is not a footprint strategy. Take old tires to a shop that recycles; do not dump them.
When you buy: a long-wear touring or all-season in the size the car came with. Lower rolling resistance can save a little fuel; read the treadwear rating so “eco” does not mean bald in 20,000 miles. Cheap no-name tires that die early mean more rubber in the gutter and more manufacturing.
Skip plus-sizing and extra-wide low-profile wheels unless you have a real reason. They often ride worse, wear faster, and cost more to replace. Winter tires are a safety tool in snow country, not a climate sin — two sets you keep for years beat one bald all-season in ice.
EVs are heavier and can wear tires faster. That does not make gasoline the greener commute (see Getting Around). It does mean inflation and a touring compound matter more.
6PPD-quinone from tire wear is a water-quality problem. There is no honest “salmon-safe” consumer tire to recommend today. Fewer miles, correct pressure, and fewer replacement sets are the levers you have.
This is not a safety inspection. If a tire is damaged, replace it.
guides.whatMattersMost: Inflate, rotate, and replace only when the tread is done. Long-wear in the original size. Fashion wheels and cheap fast-wear sets shed more rubber.
guides.commonPitfalls: Soft tires all winter. Plus-size wheels. Replacing at 6/32 because a shop upsold you. Dumping casings. Treating an EV’s faster wear as a reason to go back to gas.

keyTypes.name: Keep, Inflate & Rotate Tires
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact tire is already on the car, at the door-jamb pressure, rotated and aligned. Soft tires waste fuel and shed extra rubber — a microplastics and 6PPD problem you can cut without a new set. Pair with fewer miles in Getting Around. Replace only when the tread or damage says so.

keyTypes.name: Long-Wear Replacement Tires
keyTypes.descriptionText: When you must buy: the original size, a high treadwear rating, and rolling resistance that does not mean bald at 20,000 miles. Fewer sets over the life of the car means less manufacturing and less crumb in the gutter. Recycle the casings at the shop. Not a magic 6PPD-free product — that does not exist at the consumer counter yet.

keyTypes.name: Cheap Fast-Wear Tires
keyTypes.descriptionText: No-name rubber that disappears in a couple of seasons: more particles per mile, more factories, more dump runs. A worse deal than one good set. Bargain hunting here is not thrift. Take them to a recycler anyway when they are done.

keyTypes.name: Oversize Fashion Tires
keyTypes.descriptionText: Plus-size wheels and extra-wide low-profile tires the car did not need: harsher ride, faster shoulder wear, worse efficiency, pricey replacements. Looks are not a climate feature. Winter tires in snow country are a different decision — safety, not Instagram fitment.

guides.name: Paint
guides.descriptionText: The can you finish is cleaner than a new “zero-VOC” gallon you abandon. VOC means volatile organic compounds: solvents that evaporate as paint dries, so you breathe them indoors and they add to smog outdoors. Low-VOC latex for interiors, leftover to a reuse program, never down the drain. Pre-1978 paint can mean lead — do not dry-sand it as a weekend project.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Use what is already in the garage. Stir, strain, and finish a room before you buy another gallon. Leftover good latex can go to a Habitat-style reuse or a household hazardous-waste day — not the trash, not the gutter.
When you buy: waterborne latex or acrylic, low- or zero-VOC base (fewer of those evaporating solvents), for most indoor walls. Tint still adds some VOC; ventilate until it is dry. Eggshell or the sheen you will actually wash. Sample pots beat a five-gallon mistake.
Oil-based and strong solvents are for specific trim, floors, or metal — not a bedroom. High VOC, harder leftover, mineral spirits. Skip them as the default wall paint.
Houses built before 1978 may have lead paint. Dry-sanding or a heat gun as DIY is how dust and fumes get into kids. If the job disturbs old layers, use EPA RRP-certified work or a lead-safe method — this is not that protocol, and it is not medical advice.
Skip a full-house spray of solvent lacquer for a closet. A brush and a small can beat overspray in the lungs and the yard.
“Zero VOC” and “non-toxic” are marketing plus a test method. Biocides and colorant still exist. The honest indoor-air move is less leftover, waterborne paint, and open windows — not a miracle can.
See Cancer-Linked Chemicals for solvents and dust in the bigger picture. See Furniture if you are painting a nursery dresser that may also off-gas formaldehyde.
guides.whatMattersMost: Finish the can. Low-VOC latex for walls. Lead-safe work on old paint. Never pour leftover down the drain.
guides.commonPitfalls: A new gallon because the old one looks scary. Oil-based on every wall. Dry-sanding pre-1978 paint. “Zero VOC” as a license not to ventilate. Cans in the household trash.

keyTypes.name: Use Up Leftover Paint
keyTypes.descriptionText: The can in the garage, stirred and strained, or a reuse program that takes good latex. Manufacturing already happened. Finishing a room with leftover is the indoor-air and waste win. Unopened extras belong at hazardous waste or a recycle shop, not the alley.

keyTypes.name: Low-VOC Latex Paint
keyTypes.descriptionText: Waterborne wall paint, low- or zero-VOC base, for interiors. VOC means volatile organic compounds — the solvents that leave the can as fumes while the film dries. Tint adds some VOC; open windows until it is dry. Buy the gallons you will use. The honest upgrade from solvent paint for bedrooms and living rooms — not a reason to recast a fine wall.

keyTypes.name: Solvent Oil-Based Interior Paint
keyTypes.descriptionText: Alkyd and strong solvents as the default bedroom paint: high VOC, mineral spirits to clean, nasty leftover. Fine for a few specific jobs (some trim, metal) when the label and ventilation are real. A poor whole-room choice next to latex.

keyTypes.name: Dry-Sanding Old Lead Paint
keyTypes.descriptionText: Pre-1978 film, a sanding block, and a weekend: lead dust in the house and yard. Children and pregnant people are the high-stakes case. This is not a how-to. Hire RRP-certified work or use a lead-safe method from a public-health source — not an “eco” stripping hack. Not medical advice.

keyTypes.name: Paint Down the Drain
keyTypes.descriptionText: Leftover latex or oil poured in the sink or storm drain, or a liquid can in household trash. Solvents and biocides in water, a mess for the plant, and a wasted manufacture. Dry-out only if your city says so; otherwise hazardous-waste day or a reuse program.

guides.name: Mattresses & Pillows
guides.descriptionText: You sleep on this for a decade if you let it. Keep a sound mattress. When you buy, skip fiberglass-filled “bed-in-a-box” that dumps glass when unzipped, and skip a polyester pillow you replace every year. Flame-retardant chemistry and foam off-gassing are the indoor-air story — see Cancer-Linked Chemicals.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Keep a mattress that is still supportive and clean. Eight to ten years is a typical life, not a three-year refresh for a sale email. Rotate if the maker says to. A stain or a sag in the middle is a reason; a new Instagram bed is not.
Used mattresses are not like used dressers (see Furniture). Bedbugs and a decade of unknown treatments are real. Skip a curb mattress. A named previous owner and a thorough inspect is the only used case worth considering.
When you buy: a long-life core you can live with — natural latex, wool, or cotton (GOTS/GOLS or equivalent when you can), or a foam mattress with a current CertiPUR-style foam claim and no fiberglass. Wool is a smolder barrier that can skip extra flame-retardant soup. U.S. mattresses must meet smolder rules; they do not have to use the old additive-chemical playbook.
Do not unzip a cover that warns of fiberglass. Those “non-toxic” boxes have sent glass into bedrooms. If the spec is silent, assume risk or pick a maker that publishes “no fiberglass.”
Memory-foam-in-a-box is petroleum foam that off-gasses when new. Air it. Fine if you will keep it a long time; a cheap one every few years is Furniture’s fast-particleboard problem in sleep form.
Pillows: a washable wool, latex, or buckwheat you keep beats a polyester blob every twelve months. Down has bird-welfare and allergen questions; it lasts if you like it. Two good pillows, not a closet of hotel leftovers.
Dispose through a bulk or recycle program when you can. Do not curb a wet mattress for the next apartment.
This is not medical advice for sleep apnea or allergies. If a clinician wants a specific pillow, follow that.
guides.whatMattersMost: Years on the same sound bed. No fiberglass. Wool/latex or honest foam you keep; not a polyester pillow cycle.
guides.commonPitfalls: Unzipping a fiberglass cover. A curb mattress. Replacing a fine bed for a sale. “Non-toxic” on a mystery foam. A new poly pillow every season.

keyTypes.name: Keep a Sound Mattress
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact bed is the one already in the room that still supports you. Rotate if the maker says to. Manufacturing a mattress is a foam, steel, and fabric event — same keep-it logic as Furniture. A sale email is not a sag. Washable pillows you already like beat a new pair every year.

keyTypes.name: Latex, Wool or Cotton Mattress
keyTypes.descriptionText: A long-life core: natural latex, wool, and/or cotton, with a published standard when you can (GOLS, GOTS). Wool can serve as a smolder barrier so you skip extra flame-retardant chemistry. Costs more; only pays off if you keep it. Still a farm and factory product — not a cloud.

keyTypes.name: Certified Foam Mattress
keyTypes.descriptionText: Petroleum foam with a current emissions claim (CertiPUR-style or equivalent) and a maker who says no fiberglass. Air it when new. A fair buy if you will keep it a decade. Not a license for a new box every time the algorithm emails you. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals for the broader foam and flame-retardant picture.

keyTypes.name: Fiberglass Mattress-in-a-Box
keyTypes.descriptionText: Compressed foam with a fiberglass sock that sheds when someone unzips the cover — a documented bedroom contamination. Mystery “non-toxic” marketing, short life, a curb pile. If the spec does not say no fiberglass, treat it as this. Do not unzip to check.

keyTypes.name: Disposable Polyester Pillows
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cheap poly fill you replace when it goes flat every year or two: a small mattress of waste. Two washable wool, latex, or a decent down/synthetic you keep is the pillow version of keep-the-bed. Allergens and sleep needs are a clinician’s call, not a reason for a closet of hotel leftovers.

guides.name: Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incense
guides.descriptionText: These products do not clean air. They add perfume, solvents, and often smoke to a closed room. Open a window and fix the source (trash, litter, grease). Fragrance here is the same undisclosed-parfum problem as Cosmetics, plus combustion from candles and incense.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Smell is a clue, not a job for a plug-in. Take out the trash, wash the source, run the vent when you cook (see Gas vs Induction), crack a window. Baking soda in a fridge or a litter box is chemistry you can name.
Fragrance / parfum on an air-freshener label can hide dozens of chemicals, including some phthalates and allergens, without listing them — same blind spot as Cosmetics. “Unscented” can still include a masking scent; “fragrance-free” is the clearer claim. Essential-oil “natural” is still fragrance, and some oils irritate airways.
Skip continuous plug-ins, gels, and aerosol clouds. They dose the house all day. VOC here means volatile organic compounds: solvents that evaporate into indoor air (see Paint). People with asthma often do worse, not better. This is not medical advice — if scents trigger symptoms, talk with a clinician and stop the product.
Candles: a flame makes soot and fine particles. Paraffin plus heavy perfume is the worst common combo. Beeswax or unscented soy still smoke; they are not an air purifier. Lead wicks are banned in the U.S.; cheap imports can still be junk. Occasional dinner light is not a daily haze.
Incense is indoor combustion on purpose — high particle levels in a small room. A ceremony once in a while is a different decision from a stick with every Zoom call.
“Odor eliminating” sprays usually cover smell with more chemicals. They do not replace opening a window.
See Laundry for scent beads in clothes, and Cancer-Linked Chemicals for fragrance in the bigger picture.
guides.whatMattersMost: Clean the source and ventilate. Fragrance-free. Skip plug-ins, aerosol, daily incense, and a scented-candle habit.
guides.commonPitfalls: A plug-in as cleaning. Essential oils as unscented. Incense as meditation air. Candles as a purifier. Spraying over a litter box instead of scooping.

keyTypes.name: Open Window & Clean the Source
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact air freshener is not a product. Trash out, litter scooped, grease vented, a window cracked. You remove the smell instead of covering it. Same keep-it logic as a fridge coil: the habit beats a SKU. See Gas vs Induction for kitchen air.

keyTypes.name: Unscented Home
keyTypes.descriptionText: No plug-in, no spray, no “linens” mist. Fragrance-free detergent (see Laundry) and baking soda where a box helps. Indoor air stays the air, not a perfume formula that never has to list its parts. The default if scents bother anyone in the house.

keyTypes.name: Occasional Plain Candle
keyTypes.descriptionText: A flame for a dinner or a power outage: unscented, a stable holder, wick trimmed. Beeswax or a simple paraffin still makes particles — it is combustion. Fine rarely. Not a daily air-care routine and not an air purifier.

keyTypes.name: Plug-in & Aerosol Air Fresheners
keyTypes.descriptionText: Continuous perfume and solvents in a closed room. VOC load, undisclosed fragrance, a dose that never clocks out. Aerosols add a spray burst on top. They do not remove odor; they add chemicals. A poor trade for anyone who has to breathe the house.

keyTypes.name: Daily Incense & Scented-Candle Habit
keyTypes.descriptionText: Sticks, cones, and heavily fragranced candles as the everyday atmosphere. Indoor combustion plus perfume: fine particles and a fragrance mix you cannot read. A ceremony is one choice; a haze with every evening is a smoking indoor habit without a cigarette.

guides.name: Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant
guides.descriptionText: Daily rinse-off: the climate cost is palm oil, plastic bottles, and a twelve-product shower. Health-wise, hidden fragrance is the same Cosmetics story; you do not need antibacterial soap. A short, boring formula in a bar or a refill beats a scented aisle.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Plain soap and water clean. U.S. consumer “antibacterial” washes were pulled for a reason (triclosan and friends did not beat soap). Skip them for home hands and body.
Fragrance / parfum is still a blind mix of chemicals. Fragrance-free shampoo, bar, and deodorant are the clearer daily buy if indoor air or skin reactivity matters. Essential-oil “natural” is still scent. See Cosmetics.
A bar of soap or shampoo, or a refill into a bottle you keep, cuts plastic. Palm oil (sodium palmate and cousins) is in a lot of soap — same forest and labor story as Cooking Oils. You will not shop palm out of every bar; fewer products and a named oil help more than a leaf on the bottle.
“Sulfate-free” is not a safety ranking. Sulfates foam; some people prefer to skip them. That is comfort, not a climate trophy. A short INCI list you finish beats a five-step routine you dump.
Deodorant: a simple stick, fragrance-free if you can. Aerosol body spray is a fragrance cloud in a small bathroom. Antiperspirant (aluminum salts) is a sweat tool, not a proven cancer story — skip the internet panic, and skip this as medical advice. If a clinician has a reason for a specific product, follow that.
Microbead scrubs belong in the trash of history (see Cosmetics). A washcloth is the exfoliant.
One shampoo, one bar, one deodorant. Hotel minis and “men’s 3-in-1 plus a mist” are volume, not hygiene.
guides.whatMattersMost: Fragrance-free, short formulas, bar or refill. Skip antibacterial theater and a scented aerosol. Palm and plastic scale with how many bottles you finish.
guides.commonPitfalls: A twelve-step shower as self-care. Essential oils as fragrance-free. Antibacterial soap for Tuesday hands. Aerosol as deodorant. Treating sulfate-free as a forest offset.

keyTypes.name: Plain Bar & Short Formula
keyTypes.descriptionText: A bar of soap or shampoo, or a short fragrance-free liquid you refill. Cleans. Little plastic if you stick with the bar. Palm may still be in the fat — see Cooking Oils — but volume is low. The shower analog of Cosmetics’ “fewer products.”

keyTypes.name: Fragrance-Free Stick Deodorant
keyTypes.descriptionText: A simple stick you finish, without a parfum cloud or an aerosol can. Antiperspirant if you want less sweat; deodorant if you want less smell — that is comfort, not a cancer ranking. Not medical advice. Skip the body-spray bathroom fog.

keyTypes.name: Scented 12-Step Shower
keyTypes.descriptionText: Shampoo, conditioner, scrub, oil, 3-in-1, and a mist — most of it fragrance and palm in plastic. You rinse it to the plant. “Sulfate-free” and “clean” do not shrink the pile. One bar and one bottle beat the hotel-caddy lifestyle at home.

keyTypes.name: Antibacterial Wash & Body Spray
keyTypes.descriptionText: Theater hygiene: leftover antibacterial formulas, and aerosol deodorant that turns the bathroom into a fragrance chamber. Plain soap already works. The spray is indoor air (see Air Fresheners) plus a can. Skip both as a daily default.

guides.name: Banking & Investments
guides.descriptionText: Where the paycheck sits can dwarf a year of shopping. Deposits and retirement funds finance what banks and funds own — including fossil fuels. A credit union or a low-fee screened option is the buying guide. This is not financial advice.
guides.buyingAdvice:
This is not a stock pick, a tax plan, or a promise that markets go up. It is a comparison of where money is parked. An emergency fund you can reach still comes first.
Checking and savings: a credit union, community development bank, or a mission bank that publishes what it will not finance usually beats a megabank whose loan book underwrites new oil, gas, and coal. You do not need a brand name here — you need a deposit account that is insured (NCUA or FDIC) and a public story you can read. Moving a paycheck is paperwork; it is also leverage you do not get from a greener bottle of soap.
Retirement: look at the 401(k) menu. High-fee funds eat returns and often do not buy a better world. A low-fee broad index is honest: it owns a slice of everything, including fossil companies. A low-fee fossil-free or Paris-aligned index is a values screen with tracking difference — not a guaranteed climate outcome, and not a reason to concentrate in three “green” stocks.
“ESG” on a prospectus is unregulated marketing, like “clean beauty.” Some funds still hold oil majors. Read holdings, expense ratio, and whether the screen is actual exclusions. A sticker is not a divestment.
Do not confuse this with crypto as a climate plan (energy use is the opposite story) or with stuffing cash in a mattress. Do not yank a needed pension on a tweet.
Shareholder votes and workplace retirement-plan committees move more money than one checking account. Still: the default megabank plus an unexamined target-date fund is how a lot of households accidentally finance the thing the rest of this app is trying to shrink.
See Getting Around and Home Electricity for the physical fossil use this money is tied to.
guides.whatMattersMost: Insured deposits at a mission or credit union, then low-fee funds whose holdings you can name. ESG stickers and unexamined megabank defaults are the miss.
guides.commonPitfalls: Treating this as a hot stock tip. An ESG fund that still holds oil majors. High fees as virtue. Crypto as green. Emptying an emergency fund to “divest.”

keyTypes.name: Credit Union or Mission Bank
keyTypes.descriptionText: An insured deposit (NCUA or FDIC) at a credit union, community development bank, or a bank that publishes what it will not lend to. Your paycheck is not financing a new fossil project by default. Still a bank — not a charity. Paperwork once; impact every payday. Not financial advice.

keyTypes.name: Low-Fee Climate-Screened Funds
keyTypes.descriptionText: A retirement or brokerage option with a low expense ratio and a real exclusion list (fossil majors, coal, or a Paris-aligned benchmark you can read). Tracking will differ from the whole market. Holdings, not the ESG logo, are the product. Not a guarantee and not a concentrated “green stock” bet.

keyTypes.name: Ordinary Low-Fee Index Fund
keyTypes.descriptionText: A broad, cheap index: honest ownership of “the market,” including oil and gas. Fees are not eating you. Climate screen is none. Fine if that is all the 401(k) offers, or if you want the whole economy on purpose. Not a values product; not a rip-off either.

keyTypes.name: High-Fee ESG Sticker Fund
keyTypes.descriptionText: “Sustainable” on the cover, oil majors in the holdings, and an expense ratio that quietly taxes you. Unregulated marketing, same family as “clean beauty.” Read the top ten holdings. If you cannot name the screen, you bought a sticker.

keyTypes.name: Default Megabank & Unexamined 401k
keyTypes.descriptionText: Paycheck in a fossil-financing commercial bank, retirement in whatever target-date fund HR picked, never opened. This is how household money funds the infrastructure the rest of the app is trying to shrink. Insured and convenient — and unexamined. The avoidable case is the not-looking, not the existence of a checking account.

guides.name: Diapers
guides.descriptionText: A child goes through several thousand diapers. Disposables are plastic and superabsorbent gel headed for a landfill. Cloth only wins on climate if you wash it like laundry, not like a boil-and-bake cycle. A UK Environment Agency life-cycle study found home-washed cloth and disposables roughly similar when cloth was washed hot and partly tumble-dried — and cloth ahead with fuller, cooler loads, line-drying, and a set used for another child.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Use fewer when the child is ready. Potty learning on the child’s timeline, dry spells, and part-time cloth cut the pile the way a bidet cuts toilet paper. This is not a reason to rush anyone, and it is not medical or parenting advice. A clinician’s instructions come first.
Cloth you will actually wash. A stash of prefolds and covers — on the order of two dozen — can outfit one child and pass to the next. All-in-ones are easier and wear out sooner. Rinse solids into the toilet. Wash warm, in full loads, with the rest of the baby laundry. Line-dry. High heat spends the climate win and cooks waterproof covers. See Laundry: a hot cycle is for illness or a pail that sat, not every morning.
A diaper service is cloth without your dryer. The wash is efficient; the truck is the cost. A fair middle if line-drying will not happen.
Disposables when you need them. Many daycares require them. Overnight, travel, and no washer are real constraints. Buy plain and unscented. Fragrance on skin that stays damp is the same undisclosed-parfum problem as Cosmetics, on a baby.
Skip the green disposable. “Biodegradable,” “compostable,” and bamboo diapers are still mostly plastic plus gel, sometimes with a plant top sheet. Human waste means almost no city compost program will take them. In the trash they behave like the compostable bag in Food Storage: a claim, then a landfill. They cost more and do not close the loop.
Do not flush a diaper, cloth or disposable. Major brands are already elemental-chlorine-free; unbleached is a small extra, not the decision that matters.
guides.whatMattersMost: Fewer diapers, then cloth washed warm, line-dried, and used again. Hot tumble-drying can erase cloth’s climate edge. “Biodegradable” disposables still go to the landfill.
guides.commonPitfalls: Boiling and machine-drying every cloth load. A bamboo disposable as a finished climate plan. Scented diapers. Rushing potty learning to hit a number. Flushing anything.

keyTypes.name: Fewer Diapers When Ready
keyTypes.descriptionText: The volume cut: potty learning when the child is ready, plus dry spells and part-time cloth so you are not buying a full disposable day for years. Same idea as a bidet — use less of the product. Not a program to rush a toddler, and not medical advice. Every month shorter is thousands of plastic diapers you never buy.

keyTypes.name: Cloth, Line-Dried & Passed On
keyTypes.descriptionText: Prefolds and covers, washed warm in a full load and hung to dry, then used for another child. Manufacturing happens once. The UK Environment Agency comparison is the caution: this only beats disposables if you skip the hot tumble-dry habit. A diaper service is the same idea if you will not line-dry at home. The time is real — it usually lands on one caregiver.

keyTypes.name: Plain Unscented Disposables
keyTypes.descriptionText: The honest fallback: daycare rules, overnight, travel, no washer. One-use plastic and gel, landfilled, several thousand times. Climate can look like badly washed cloth; the trash does not. Unscented, no lotion. Fragrance on damp skin is a cosmetics problem with a smaller customer. Not a moral failing when cloth is not available.

keyTypes.name: Hot-Wash, Tumble-Dry Cloth
keyTypes.descriptionText: Cloth in name, disposable in energy. A hot half-load and a long dry cycle is the scenario where the UK Environment Agency found reusable diapers no better on greenhouse gases than disposables — sometimes the electricity wins. Waterproof covers wear out. Wash warm and full, and line-dry, or you bought the work without the climate result. See Laundry.

keyTypes.name: “Biodegradable” & Scented Disposables
keyTypes.descriptionText: Bamboo, “plant-based,” and compostable diapers that still go in the trash, often with fragrance. Almost no municipal compost site accepts human waste, so the end of life is a landfill, same as a normal diaper. You paid extra for a top sheet and a claim. Scent adds undisclosed fragrance on infant skin. Buy plain unscented if you need a disposable.

guides.name: Cut Flowers
guides.descriptionText: A bouquet is a perishable crop, then a flight or a heated greenhouse, then a week in a vase. Field flowers grown near you, in season, beat both. A UK comparison of roses found fossil-heated greenhouse stems higher-carbon than roses flown from East Africa — the heat cost more than the plane — and local seasonal stems beat both. A sleeve printed in your town does not mean the roses grew there.
guides.buyingAdvice:
Buy what is blooming near you. A named local farm, a farmers-market bucket, or a flower CSA in season: zinnias, dahlias, sunflowers, peonies, branches. Field-grown and trucked. You can ask what was sprayed. See Produce for the same in-season logic on food.
Keep something. A potted plant you actually keep, dried local stems, or branches from a yard you already tend outlast a weekly wrap. One plant beats a year of bouquets.
If you want roses out of season, read the standard. Fair Trade, or an equivalent published label rather than a shop’s “responsibly grown,” is the labor and pesticide floor on an imported stem. The flight is still there. Kenya and Ethiopia supply a lot of European roses; Colombia and Ecuador supply most roses in the U.S. A Fair Trade flown rose can still be lower-carbon than a rose from a fossil-heated glasshouse.
“Holland” is often the auction, not the farm. Dutch markets move flowers grown elsewhere. A stem traded through the Netherlands is a different product from one raised under heated Dutch glass.
Skip floral foam. The green brick, often sold as Oasis, is plastic foam. It sheds microplastics, does not compost, and does not belong in the garden. A vase you own, a tape grid, chicken wire, or a flower frog holds stems without it.
Unlabeled imported bunches, especially holiday roses, are the avoidable default: air freight, cosmetic pesticides on a crop nobody eats, opaque wages, a plastic sleeve. The harm is worker exposure and local water, not a rose on the table poisoning you.
A funeral or a hospital visit is not the decision this guide is for. The weekly habit is.
guides.whatMattersMost: Season and distance first: local field flowers, or a plant you keep. A fossil-heated greenhouse can cost more carbon than a flight. Fair Trade is the labor floor on imported stems, not a climate offset.
guides.commonPitfalls: A town florist’s sleeve on flowers that flew in. “Holland” as proof they were grown in Holland. Floral foam in the garden. A weekly imported rose habit. Treating Fair Trade as permission to ignore the plane.

keyTypes.name: Seasonal Local Stems
keyTypes.descriptionText: What a nearby farm is cutting this week: zinnias, dahlias, sunflowers, peonies, branches. Field-grown, trucked, and you can ask who grew them. The climate win is skipping the airplane and the heated glasshouse. Money stays with the grower. A week in a jar, then the compost — that is the product, bought on purpose.

keyTypes.name: A Plant You Keep
keyTypes.descriptionText: The lowest-impact bouquet is one you do not replace. A plant already in the house, dried stems, or yard branches. A hardy pot you will still water next year beats a poinsettia that dies in January. Growing once, keeping it, is the same logic as a bottle you refill.

keyTypes.name: Fair Trade Flown Roses
keyTypes.descriptionText: Roses grown for export — often East Africa or the Andes — and flown because they wilt. Fairtrade (or a standard you can actually read) covers wages and some pesticide rules. It is the better imported bunch. It is still a flight. A UK rose comparison found this kind of bloom lower-carbon than fossil-heated Dutch glass, and higher than a local field. Water and the airplane remain.

keyTypes.name: Fossil-Heated Greenhouse Blooms
keyTypes.descriptionText: Roses and other cuts forced in cold-climate glass on fossil heat. The published UK comparison found this higher-carbon than roses flown from Kenya: months of heating outweighed the airplane. Pretty, local-feeling, and energy-hungry. A greenhouse on waste heat or renewables is a different claim — the stem does not say so unless the grower does.

keyTypes.name: Uncertified Imported Bouquet
keyTypes.descriptionText: The default grocery or holiday bunch: flown stems, no named farm, no labor standard, often a plastic sleeve and a brick of floral foam. Flowers are not food, so produce-style residue rules often do not apply. The harm that shows up is workers and runoff, plus a week of trash. “Biodegradable foam” still is not a home compost. Ask for a jar of water and a bunch you can trace, or wait for the local farm.

guides.name: Menstrual Products
guides.descriptionText: Over a lifetime this is thousands of products. A cup, a disc, or a washable pad used for years beats a monthly box. “Organic” and “bamboo” disposables are still single-use. Fragrance does not belong here.
guides.buyingAdvice:
A menstrual cup or reusable disc in medical-grade silicone is the usual lowest-waste option when it fits your body and your bathroom. Makers often rate one cup for up to a decade. Boil between cycles. Wash with unscented soap during. Follow the hours in the leaflet. This is not medical advice. If you have an IUD, ask the clinician who placed it before you use a cup. Toxic shock is rare. It is about time and absorbency, including with cups. Organic cotton does not remove it.
Cloth pads and period underwear go in a normal load and hang to dry. See Laundry: not a hot half-empty cycle, and no softener. A lot of underwear is polyester, so it can shed microfibers. Some brands have tested high for fluorine, a PFAS marker. Buy one that publishes a third-party PFAS test. See Cancer-Linked Chemicals.
Disposables when you need them: travel, postpartum, a bathroom with no privacy, a school day. Unscented. A cardboard applicator, or none. A plastic applicator is a second piece of trash. Tampons are less plastic than a pad with a plastic back. “Organic cotton” is better farming and still one product every few hours. A 2024 lab study found metals, including lead, in both organic and conventional tampons. It did not show those metals leaving the tampon into the body. That is not a reason to panic, and it is not a reason to treat organic as a detox.
Skip “biodegradable” and bamboo disposables as a climate plan. Many still have a plastic leak-proof sheet. Blood means almost no city compost program will take them. In the trash they are the diaper problem again. See Diapers.
Skip fragrance and “odor” liners. Scent here is the Cosmetics parfum problem in a worse place. It does not clean.
A pad from a pantry or a clinic is the right product that day. The decision is the monthly habit you can change.
guides.whatMattersMost: A cup, disc, or washable pad you will actually use for years. Unscented disposables when reusables will not work. Organic, bamboo, and scented plastic are not the upgrade.
guides.commonPitfalls: Organic cotton as a finished plan. Bamboo pads in the compost. Scented products. Period underwear with no published PFAS test. A cup you boil and a box of plastic pads you still buy every month.
