keyTypes.name: Menstrual Cup or Reusable Disc
keyTypes.descriptionText: Medical-grade silicone, boiled between cycles, often rated for up to ten years. Manufacturing happens once. You need clean hands and a bathroom where you can empty it. Follow the hours in the leaflet. If you have an IUD, ask the clinician who placed it first. This is not medical advice. The lowest-waste option when it actually works for you.

keyTypes.name: Cloth Pads & Period Underwear
keyTypes.descriptionText: Washable pads or underwear in a normal laundry load, hung to dry. No softener. Years of use instead of a box a month. Polyester underwear sheds microfibers, and some brands have tested high for fluorine, a PFAS marker — buy one that publishes a third-party test. See Laundry and Cancer-Linked Chemicals. A strong choice when a cup is not going to happen.

keyTypes.name: Unscented Cotton Disposables
keyTypes.descriptionText: The honest fallback: travel, postpartum, school, a bathroom with no privacy. Unscented tampons or pads, cardboard applicator or none. Less waste than a plastic-backed scented pad, and still thousands of products over a lifetime. Organic cotton is better farming, not a detox. A 2024 lab study found metals in both organic and conventional tampons and did not show them leaching into the body.

keyTypes.name: “Biodegradable” & Bamboo Disposables
keyTypes.descriptionText: A monthly box with a leaf on it. Many bamboo or “compostable” pads still have a plastic leak-proof layer. Blood means almost no municipal compost site will take them, so the end of life is the trash, same as a normal pad. You paid extra for a claim. See Diapers. Unscented cotton, or a reusable, is the clearer buy.

keyTypes.name: Plastic Pads & Scented Products
keyTypes.descriptionText: The default aisle: a plastic-backed pad, a plastic applicator, a wrapper, and often fragrance. Thousands of them, then a landfill. Scent on this skin does not clean and hides whatever is in “parfum.” See Cosmetics. A pantry pad in an emergency is not this habit. The habit is buying it every month when a reusable or an unscented tampon was available.

Everyday Protein.name: Environmental Working Group — Meat Eater’s Guide (2011)
Everyday Protein.detail: U.S. life-cycle estimates this guide’s protein figures follow: beef about 27 kg CO₂e per kg eaten, chicken about 6.9, beans and lentils near 1.

Everyday Protein.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Everyday Protein.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Everyday Protein.name: Water Footprint Network
Everyday Protein.detail: The large water figures for beef (on the order of 15,000 liters per kilogram) come from Mekonnen & Hoekstra’s global water-footprint accounts, not from a local farm’s meter.

Seafood.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch
Seafood.detail: The green / yellow / red ratings this guide uses. Stock, gear, and country change the color, so the species name on a menu is not enough.

Seafood.name: Marine Stewardship Council
Seafood.detail: The blue label for a wild fishery that passed an independent stock and bycatch assessment. It is a useful mark, not a substitute for checking origin.

Milk.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Milk.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Milk.name: Environmental Working Group — Meat Eater’s Guide (2011)
Milk.detail: U.S. life-cycle estimates this guide’s protein figures follow: beef about 27 kg CO₂e per kg eaten, chicken about 6.9, beans and lentils near 1.

Eggs.name: ASPCA — meat, eggs, and dairy label guide
Eggs.detail: What “pasture-raised,” “free-range,” and “cage-free” do and do not mean. A local carton is not outdoor access unless the flock actually goes outside.

Eggs.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Eggs.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Coffee.name: Fairtrade International
Coffee.detail: The common grocery standard for a minimum price, a premium, and rules on child labor and cooperatives. It is a floor, not a guarantee that every audit catches every farm.

Coffee.name: Smithsonian’s National Zoo — Bird Friendly coffee
Coffee.detail: Shade-grown coffee that keeps forest cover and bird habitat. “Local” for coffee means a transparent roaster; the beans still grow in the tropics.

Produce.name: Our World in Data — food choice vs. eating local
Produce.detail: Transport is a small share of most foods’ climate cost. The exceptions are air freight and, for some crops, heated greenhouses.

Produce.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Produce.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Chocolate.name: U.S. Department of Labor — child labor in cocoa
Chocolate.detail: The long-running documentation of child labor in West African cocoa, which is where most of the world’s beans are grown.

Chocolate.name: Fairtrade International
Chocolate.detail: The common grocery standard for a minimum price, a premium, and rules on child labor and cooperatives. It is a floor, not a guarantee that every audit catches every farm.

Chocolate.name: U.S. FDA — environmental contaminants in food
Chocolate.detail: Lead and cadmium show up in some cocoa solids. That is a reason to vary brands, not a reason to treat a square of chocolate as an emergency.

Cooking Oils.name: World Wildlife Fund — palm oil
Cooking Oils.detail: Palm yields a lot of oil per acre, which is why it is cheap and why clearing tropical forest and peat for it is so damaging.

Cooking Oils.name: Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil
Cooking Oils.detail: The common certification for palm in packaged food. It is a floor when you cannot avoid palm, not a reason to seek it out.

Cooking Oils.name: UC Davis Olive Center
Cooking Oils.detail: Testing and buying guidance on olive oil fraud: “packed in Italy” is not the same as crushed there.

Pasta.name: PAN Europe — TFA in grain products (2026)
Pasta.detail: Testing of 66 grain samples from 16 countries found TFA, a PFAS breakdown product, in 54 — highest in wheat products. An emerging concern this guide watches rather than ranks on.

Pasta.name: Environmental Working Group — Food Scores
Pasta.detail: EWG’s pasta pages show the nutrition, ingredient, and processing breakdown this guide’s health angle follows.

Pasta.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Pasta.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Bread.name: Florida Department of Agriculture — bread testing (2026)
Bread.detail: State testing found glyphosate at 587 ppb in a major brand’s 100% whole wheat loaf and non-detect in the same brand’s white loaf — the whole-grain residue paradox this guide flags.

Bread.name: PAN Europe — TFA in grain products (2026)
Bread.detail: TFA residues were also detected in bread rolls in the same 66-sample study cited in the Pasta guide.

Bread.name: Shepherd’s Grain — published residue testing
Bread.detail: A regional flour cooperative that publishes twice-yearly tests against EU glyphosate limits; the transparency model this guide rewards.

Breakfast Cereal.name: Environmental Working Group — Food Scores
Breakfast Cereal.detail: EWG’s nutrition, ingredient, and processing concern scores are the methodology this guide’s health ranking follows.

Breakfast Cereal.name: Environmental Working Group — glyphosate in oat products
Breakfast Cereal.detail: EWG-commissioned testing found glyphosate in nearly all conventional oat cereals and snack bars sampled, the finding behind the organic recommendation.

Breakfast Cereal.name: World Wildlife Fund — palm oil
Breakfast Cereal.detail: Palm yields a lot of oil per acre, which is why it is cheap and why clearing tropical forest and peat for it is so damaging.

Peanut Butter.name: World Wildlife Fund — palm oil
Peanut Butter.detail: Palm yields a lot of oil per acre, which is why it is cheap and why clearing tropical forest and peat for it is so damaging.

Peanut Butter.name: Global Witness — palm oil and deforestation (2026)
Peanut Butter.detail: Linked tainted palm oil from Papua New Guinea clearances to household brands and their financiers — the supply-chain opacity this guide penalizes.

Peanut Butter.name: U.S. Customs and Border Protection — Withhold Release Orders (Sept 2026)
Peanut Butter.detail: CBP blocked palm oil from two Indonesian producers over forced-labor findings — evidence the labor risk in uncertified palm oil is current, not historical.

Tea.name: Fairtrade International
Tea.detail: The common grocery standard for a minimum price, a premium, and rules on child labor and cooperatives. It is a floor, not a guarantee that every audit catches every farm.

Tea.name: Ethical Consumer — tea guide
Tea.detail: Their tea rankings weigh plantation wages and pesticide use; cited here for the labor-first ordering of this guide.

Rice & Grains.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Rice & Grains.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Rice & Grains.name: Arsenic in rice — FDA / EWG guidance
Rice & Grains.detail: Regulators advise rinsing rice and varying grains, especially for children; the reason this appears in the advice rather than the scores.

Sodas.name: Dietary Guidelines for Americans — added sugars
Sodas.detail: Federal guidance caps added sugars at under 10% of daily calories; a single 12-oz soda is most of a day’s allowance. The health-first ordering of this guide follows that.

Sodas.name: Sugar supply chains — cane, beet, and corn
Sodas.detail: Sugar production carries documented land, water, and labor costs on several continents; sweetener origin is why cane and corn syrup are scored apart here.

Energy Drinks.name: American Academy of Pediatrics — energy drinks and adolescents
Energy Drinks.detail: The AAP’s position is that energy drinks have no place in the diet of children and adolescents — the basis for this guide’s social score.

Energy Drinks.name: U.S. FDA — caffeine guidance
Energy Drinks.detail: The FDA cites 400 mg of caffeine a day as a level not generally associated with negative effects for healthy adults; many single cans approach that.

Juice & Dried Fruit.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Juice & Dried Fruit.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Juice & Dried Fruit.name: Dietary Guidelines for Americans — juice vs. whole fruit
Juice & Dried Fruit.detail: Federal guidance counts 100% juice as fruit but advises that at least half of fruit intake be whole, because juice drops the fiber and concentrates the sugar.

Canned & Frozen Vegetables.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Canned & Frozen Vegetables.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Canned & Frozen Vegetables.name: Can linings and BPA — EWG reporting
Canned & Frozen Vegetables.detail: EWG’s canned-food testing found BPA in many can linings; BPA-free-lined cans are the preference stated in this guide, with steel’s recyclability as the offsetting plus.

Light Bulbs.name: U.S. Department of Energy — LED basics
Light Bulbs.detail: LEDs use a fraction of the electricity of incandescent bulbs and last far longer. Compare lumens, not the old watt number.

Light Bulbs.name: U.S. EPA — compact fluorescent bulbs
Light Bulbs.detail: CFLs contain a small amount of mercury and should be recycled as hazardous waste, not tossed in the kitchen trash.

Home Electricity.name: U.S. Department of Energy — homeowner’s guide to solar
Home Electricity.detail: How rooftop solar is sized, and why tightening the house’s energy use comes before covering the roof with panels.

Home Electricity.name: U.S. EPA — eGRID
Home Electricity.detail: The inventory of how carbon-intensive the U.S. grid is, by region. That is the electricity a panel or an efficiency upgrade displaces.

Getting Around.name: Our World in Data — travel carbon footprint
Getting Around.detail: Per-passenger emissions for flying, driving, rail, and bus. Miles and mode dominate; the brand of the vehicle does not.

Getting Around.name: U.S. EPA — transportation and climate
Getting Around.detail: Transportation is a top share of U.S. greenhouse gases, mostly from passenger cars and trucks.

Smartphones.name: Apple — environment
Smartphones.detail: Product reports for phones show most of the climate cost in manufacturing, not in charging. Keeping a working phone skips that cycle. Other makers publish the same pattern.

Smartphones.name: U.S. EPA — electronics donation and recycling
Smartphones.detail: Where a retired phone should go, and why boards do not belong in household trash.

Water Bottles.name: U.S. EPA — reducing waste
Water Bottles.detail: The practical case for skipping single-use bottles. A bottle you actually carry replaces a long chain of new plastic.

Household Cleaners.name: U.S. EPA — Safer Choice
Household Cleaners.detail: A federal label for cleaning ingredients that meet published health and environmental criteria. Concentrates and refills cut the packaging on top of that.

Shopping Bags.name: UK Environment Agency — supermarket carrier bags
Shopping Bags.detail: The 2011 life-cycle review: a bag’s impact depends on how many times you use it. An unused cotton tote can lose to a thin bag you reuse.

Clothing.name: Ellen MacArthur Foundation — A New Textiles Economy
Clothing.detail: The case that clothing’s waste problem is making garments that are barely worn. Wearing what you own, and buying used, is the main cut.

Clothing.name: Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS)
Clothing.detail: Organic fiber plus dyeing and labor rules for textiles. Organic cotton is better farming; a closet of new organic shirts is still a manufacture cycle.

Clothing.name: Textile Exchange — preferred fibers
Clothing.detail: Comparative reporting on cotton, wool, down, polyester, and man-made cellulosics, including water, chemistry, and the standards behind recycled or certified fibers.

Summer Clothing.name: Textile Exchange — preferred fibers
Summer Clothing.detail: Comparative reporting on cotton, wool, down, polyester, and man-made cellulosics, including water, chemistry, and the standards behind recycled or certified fibers.

Summer Clothing.name: Lenzing — TENCEL lyocell
Summer Clothing.detail: Lyocell’s lower-impact claim is the closed-loop solvent process. Generic viscose or rayon is a different fiber with a different chemical trail.

Winter Clothing.name: Textile Exchange — Responsible Wool Standard
Winter Clothing.detail: The animal-welfare and land standard to look for on new wool.

Winter Clothing.name: Textile Exchange — Responsible Down Standard
Winter Clothing.detail: The traceable down standard. Down still has to stay dry; a wet puffer without a shell is not a winter system.

Winter Clothing.name: National Weather Service — winter safety
Winter Clothing.detail: Layering is the cold-weather practice this guide follows. Cotton holds water and stops insulating once it is wet.

Outdoor Clothing.name: Textile Exchange — preferred fibers
Outdoor Clothing.detail: Comparative reporting on cotton, wool, down, polyester, and man-made cellulosics, including water, chemistry, and the standards behind recycled or certified fibers.

Outdoor Clothing.name: Green Science Policy Institute
Outdoor Clothing.detail: Research on PFAS in water-repellent finishes. A recycled shell with a PFAS-free durable water repellent is the better new rain layer.

Outdoor Clothing.name: National Weather Service — winter safety
Outdoor Clothing.detail: Cotton next to the skin while you are working in wind or wet cold is treated as a safety problem, not a style choice.

Shoes.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Shoes.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Shoes.name: Textile Exchange — preferred fibers
Shoes.detail: Leather is a cattle product, so it carries the land story of beef. Years of wear, and a resole, matter more than a new pair’s material claim.

Kayaks.name: American Canoe Association
Kayaks.detail: Hull length, rocker, and flotation are how paddling instruction describes tracking, turning, and rough water. This guide follows that design language.

Kayaks.name: How the material ranking was made
Kayaks.detail: There is no public life-cycle study these kayak scores are copied from. The order compares how the hull is made — PVC, polyethylene, composites, wood — and whether you keep the boat for years.

Sunscreens.name: U.S. FDA — sunscreen
Sunscreens.detail: Broad spectrum, SPF, and water resistance are defined on the Drug Facts label. “Reef safe” on the front of the bottle is not a regulated term.

Sunscreens.name: American Academy of Dermatology — sunscreen
Sunscreens.detail: How much to use and when to reapply. SPF 50 is not twice SPF 30, and no bottle replaces shade and a shirt.

Sunscreens.name: NOAA — sunscreen chemicals and corals
Sunscreens.detail: Why oxybenzone and octinoxate are the filters this guide tells you to skip near reefs. Hawaii, Palau, and the U.S. Virgin Islands restrict them.

Bug Repellents.name: U.S. EPA — insect repellents
Bug Repellents.detail: The registered skin actives with evidence: DEET, picaridin, IR3535, and oil of lemon eucalyptus (PMD). The label concentration is the duration.

Bug Repellents.name: U.S. CDC — mosquitoes
Bug Repellents.detail: CDC’s recommended repellents match that EPA list. Essential-oil mists are not the plan where mosquito- or tick-borne disease is the risk.

Bug Repellents.name: U.S. EPA — permethrin-treated clothing
Bug Repellents.detail: The EPA repellent page covers permethrin on fabric and gear: not for skin, and kept away from cats while it is wet.

Cancer-Linked Chemicals.name: U.S. CDC — tobacco
Cancer-Linked Chemicals.detail: Smoking remains the leading preventable cause of cancer in the United States. That outranks a trace warning on a shampoo bottle.

Cancer-Linked Chemicals.name: U.S. EPA — radon
Cancer-Linked Chemicals.detail: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer overall and the leading cause among people who do not smoke. A short-term test kit is the check.

Cancer-Linked Chemicals.name: World Health Organization — red and processed meat
Cancer-Linked Chemicals.detail: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1). The guide treats that as “rare, not breakfast,” not as a ban on a single hot dog.

Cancer-Linked Chemicals.name: California OEHHA — Proposition 65
Cancer-Linked Chemicals.detail: The warning is a legal notice that a chemical is on a list. It is not a ranked risk, and it shows up on products with very different doses.

Cancer-Linked Chemicals.name: U.S. EPA — PFAS
Cancer-Linked Chemicals.detail: The “forever chemical” family used in some nonstick coatings, stain guards, and long-wear cosmetics. A published third-party test is the way to check a product claim.

Lawn Care.name: U.S. EPA — nutrient pollution
Lawn Care.detail: Fertilizer, especially phosphorus, that runs off turf feeds algae in lakes and bays. Many lawns already have enough phosphorus.

Lawn Care.name: U.S. EPA — lawn and garden pest control
Lawn Care.detail: Spot treatment instead of a whole-yard spray, and the label’s wait time before people and pets go back on the grass.

Lawn Care.name: Xerces Society — neonicotinoids
Lawn Care.detail: Why broadcast “insect control” granules are a problem for bees and other insects beyond the grub you meant to hit.

Cosmetics.name: U.S. FDA — fragrances in cosmetics
Cosmetics.detail: “Fragrance” or “parfum” on a label can stand in for a mixture of chemicals that are not listed one by one.

Cosmetics.name: U.S. EPA — PFAS
Cosmetics.detail: The “forever chemical” family used in some nonstick coatings, stain guards, and long-wear cosmetics. A published third-party test is the way to check a product claim.

Cosmetics.name: Leaping Bunny
Cosmetics.detail: The cruelty-free standard this guide means. It is about animal testing, not about whether the formula is safer or lower impact.

Cosmetics.name: Responsible Mica Initiative
Cosmetics.detail: Child labor in some mica mines, and the case for brands that trace mica or use a synthetic substitute.

Laundry.name: ENERGY STAR — clothes washers
Laundry.detail: Heating the water is most of a wash cycle’s energy. Cold water and a full load are the levers; the scent of the bottle is not.

Laundry.name: NOAA — microplastics
Laundry.detail: Synthetic clothes shed fibers in the wash. Washing less often, on cold, in a fuller load, sheds fewer of them.

Gas vs Induction.name: Stanford Report — gas and propane stoves
Gas vs Induction.detail: Stanford’s indoor-air measurements: gas stoves emit nitrogen dioxide and leak methane even aside from the flame. Electric burners do not make NO₂.

Gas vs Induction.name: U.S. EPA — indoor air quality
Gas vs Induction.detail: Combustion, fragrance, and solvents add pollutants inside the house. Ventilation and fewer products beat a cover-up spray.

Refrigerators.name: ENERGY STAR — refrigerators
Refrigerators.detail: Top-freezer models generally use less electricity than side-by-side and through-door ice dispensers. A working fridge you keep beats a new sticker.

Refrigerators.name: U.S. EPA — refrigerant management
Refrigerators.detail: Old refrigerants are powerful greenhouse gases. A disposal program should recover them rather than venting the system.

Furniture.name: U.S. EPA — composite wood formaldehyde
Furniture.detail: TSCA Title VI limits formaldehyde from particleboard, MDF, and hardwood plywood sold in the U.S. Air a new piece before it lives in a bedroom.

Furniture.name: Forest Stewardship Council
Furniture.detail: The chain-of-custody label for wood from a managed forest. A tropical hardwood with no paperwork is not that label.

Laptops & Computers.name: Apple — environment
Laptops & Computers.detail: As with phones, published computer footprints are mostly manufacturing. Extra RAM or storage that keeps a machine in service avoids a new one.

Laptops & Computers.name: iFixit
Laptops & Computers.detail: Repairability scores and parts. A machine you can open is the one you can keep when the battery or drive fails.

Laptops & Computers.name: U.S. EPA — electronics donation and recycling
Laptops & Computers.detail: Wipe the drive, then use a certified recycler. Boards are not household trash.

Toilet Paper & Paper Towels.name: NRDC — The Issue with Tissue
Toilet Paper & Paper Towels.detail: The scorecard linking ultra-plush virgin toilet paper to the boreal forest, and the case for recycled content and using less.

Toilet Paper & Paper Towels.name: U.S. EPA — reducing waste
Toilet Paper & Paper Towels.detail: A bidet, a rag, and a recycled roll all cut a product that is used once. “Flushable” wipes are a pipe problem, not a forest solution.

Pet Food.name: WSAVA — global nutrition guidelines
Pet Food.detail: What “complete and balanced” is supposed to mean. Cats are obligate carnivores. A homemade vegan diet is not a climate plan for a cat.

Pet Food.name: AAFCO
Pet Food.detail: The U.S. profiles pet-food labels cite. A novel-protein or lower-meat diet for a dog is a formulated food, not table scraps.

Pet Food.name: U.S. FDA — raw pet food
Pet Food.detail: Raw diets can spread Salmonella in the kitchen, and they use a lot of meat that could have been a complete cooked food.

Pet Food.name: Our World in Data — environmental impacts of food
Pet Food.detail: Readable summary of Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018), the large comparison of greenhouse gases, land, and water across foods. Beef and dairy sit far above chicken and plants.

Food Storage.name: FTC Green Guides — compostable claims
Food Storage.detail: How “compostable” and “biodegradable” claims are supposed to work. A bag that only breaks down in an industrial facility you do not have is still trash.

Food Storage.name: U.S. EPA — reducing waste
Food Storage.detail: Eating the leftover, and reusing a jar you already own, beats manufacturing a new container.

Batteries.name: U.S. EPA — used household batteries
Batteries.detail: Which cells can wait for ordinary recycling and which (lithium, button cells, lead-acid) need a dedicated drop-off. Lithium does not go in the kitchen bin.

Batteries.name: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — button batteries
Batteries.detail: Coin cells are a swallowing emergency for children. They are also not a NiMH rechargeable you can casually swap.

Dishwashing.name: ENERGY STAR — dishwashers
Dishwashing.detail: A full certified dishwasher typically uses less water and energy than washing the same load under a running tap. Heated dry and a pre-rinse spend the savings.

Tires.name: U.S. EPA — 6PPD and 6PPD-quinone
Tires.detail: The tire antioxidant that becomes 6PPD-quinone, a chemical that kills coho salmon in stormwater. EPA is still asking for alternatives; a shopper cannot yet buy a tire without it.

Tires.name: NHTSA — tires
Tires.detail: Replace for tread and damage, not for a shop’s upsell. U.S. passenger tires are worn out at 2/32 inch. Inflation and rotation are the wear you can control.

Paint.name: U.S. EPA — volatile organic compounds
Paint.detail: VOCs are solvents that evaporate into indoor air and outdoor smog. Low-VOC paint and fewer fresheners cut that dose; they do not make a product zero.

Paint.name: U.S. EPA — lead renovation, repair, and painting
Paint.detail: Homes built before 1978 may have lead paint. Dry-sanding or heat-gunning it is how lead dust gets into a house. Disturbed work belongs with an RRP-certified contractor.

Mattresses & Pillows.name: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — mattresses
Mattresses & Pillows.detail: Federal smolder standards for mattresses. Meeting them does not require a fiberglass fire barrier.

Mattresses & Pillows.name: CertiPUR-US
Mattresses & Pillows.detail: A foam-content standard some bed-in-a-box makers cite. It is not a test of the whole mattress, and it does not mean “no fiberglass.”

Mattresses & Pillows.name: Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS)
Mattresses & Pillows.detail: Organic fiber plus dyeing and labor rules for textiles. Organic cotton is better farming; a closet of new organic shirts is still a manufacture cycle.

Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.name: U.S. EPA — volatile organic compounds
Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.detail: VOCs are solvents that evaporate into indoor air and outdoor smog. Low-VOC paint and fewer fresheners cut that dose; they do not make a product zero.

Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.name: U.S. FDA — fragrances in cosmetics
Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.detail: “Fragrance” or “parfum” on a label can stand in for a mixture of chemicals that are not listed one by one.

Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.name: U.S. EPA — indoor air quality
Air Fresheners, Scented Candles & Incens.detail: Combustion, fragrance, and solvents add pollutants inside the house. Ventilation and fewer products beat a cover-up spray.

Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.name: U.S. FDA — skip antibacterial soap
Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.detail: The 2016 rule: consumer antibacterial washes with triclosan and similar ingredients did not beat plain soap and water.

Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.name: U.S. FDA — fragrances in cosmetics
Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.detail: “Fragrance” or “parfum” on a label can stand in for a mixture of chemicals that are not listed one by one.

Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.name: World Wildlife Fund — palm oil
Shampoo, Soap & Deodorant.detail: Palm yields a lot of oil per acre, which is why it is cheap and why clearing tropical forest and peat for it is so damaging.

Banking & Investments.name: Banking on Climate Chaos
Banking & Investments.detail: The annual tally of bank financing for fossil fuels, from Rainforest Action Network and partner nonprofits. It is why a default megabank is not a neutral place to park a paycheck.

Banking & Investments.name: NCUA — share insurance
Banking & Investments.detail: Credit union deposits are insured up to the federal limit. A mission bank should still be FDIC-insured. This guide is not advice about returns.

Banking & Investments.name: FDIC — deposit insurance
Banking & Investments.detail: The insurance backstop for bank deposits. Moving money to a smaller institution does not mean giving that up.

Diapers.name: UK Environment Agency — disposable and reusable nappies (2008)
Diapers.detail: The life-cycle study this guide describes. Home-washed cloth and disposables were similar when cloth was washed hot and partly tumble-dried. Fuller, cooler loads, line-drying, and a second child moved cloth ahead.

Cut Flowers.name: Cranfield University — roses from Kenya and the Netherlands (2007)
Cut Flowers.detail: The comparison this guide uses, summarized by Table Debates: fossil-heated Dutch greenhouse roses had several times the climate cost of roses flown from Kenya. Season and heat can outweigh the flight.

Cut Flowers.name: Fairtrade International
Cut Flowers.detail: The common grocery standard for a minimum price, a premium, and rules on child labor and cooperatives. It is a floor, not a guarantee that every audit catches every farm.

Menstrual Products.name: Shearston et al., Environment International (2024)
Menstrual Products.detail: The lab study that found metals, including lead, in both organic and conventional tampons. It did not show those metals leaving the tampon and entering the body. Columbia’s summary is the public write-up.

Menstrual Products.name: U.S. EPA — PFAS
Menstrual Products.detail: The “forever chemical” family used in some nonstick coatings, stain guards, and long-wear cosmetics. A published third-party test is the way to check a product claim.

Menstrual Products.name: FTC Green Guides — compostable claims
Menstrual Products.detail: “Biodegradable” and “compostable” claims. Menstrual products with blood are not accepted by ordinary city compost programs.
